# How to use this guide

Nursing Foundation II (including the 40-hour Health Assessment Module) is the second-semester core nursing course of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum: 6 credits (120 hours) of theory, 3 credits (120 hours) of skill lab and 4 credits (320 hours) of clinical practice in medical and surgical wards. It turns the basics of Nursing Foundation I into bedside skills — assessment, the nursing process, feeding, hygiene, elimination, oxygen, fluids, medicines, care of the unconscious and dying, and psychosocial care.

**One paper for Foundation I and II.** Nursing Foundation I (first semester) has no university exam of its own. At the end of the second semester you sit **one 3-hour, 75-mark university paper, "Nursing Foundations (I & II)"**, listed in the INC tables as "Nursing Foundations II including First Aid". Questions may come from **both** courses. The internal assessment (25 marks) is the average of the Foundation I and Foundation II internal marks. This pack covers the whole Foundation II syllabus and adds the **First Aid unit of Foundation I** (Unit 10 here), because the paper names first aid. Revise the other Foundation I topics — health and illness, history of nursing, communication, documentation, vital signs, infection control, comfort, pain, sleep, admission and discharge, mobility and patient education — from the Nursing Foundation I pack.

**How the units are arranged.** The INC syllabus for Foundation II has sixteen units. Small units are joined so that each notes file is a useful size:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Hours (theory + skill lab) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Health assessment | I | 20 + 20 |
| Unit 2 Nursing process and nursing theories | II + XVI | 13 + 8; 6 |
| Unit 3 Nutritional needs and hygiene | III + IV | 5 + 5; 5 + 15 |
| Unit 4 Elimination needs and diagnostic testing | V + VI | 10 + 10; 3 + 4 |
| Unit 5 Oxygenation needs | VII | 11 + 10 |
| Unit 6 Fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance | VIII | 5 + 10 |
| Unit 7 Administration of medications | IX | 20 + 22 |
| Unit 8 Sensory needs, unconscious patient, death and dying | X + XI | 5 + 6; 4 + 6 |
| Unit 9 Psychosocial needs | XII–XV | 3; 2; 2 + 4; 6 |
| Unit 10 First aid and emergencies | Foundation I, Unit XIV | 20 + 20 |

Procedures are written as the steps you learn in the skill lab, each with its reason. Medication administration is taught as principles — the rights, routes, sites and the calculation method. The calculation examples use invented drugs and numbers for practice only; no drug doses are given anywhere in this pack.

**The university paper (75 marks, 3 hours)** — the pattern given in INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3, for a full 75-mark paper. There is no internal choice: answer every question. Your university may print it differently; confirm with your university.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 12 multiple-choice questions | 12 × 1 = 12 |
| Essay / situation type | 2 long answers | 2 × 15 = 30 |
| Short | 5 short answers | 5 × 5 = 25 |
| Very short | 4 very short answers | 4 × 2 = 8 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

Theory total is 100 (75 university + 25 internal); you need at least 50% in theory. The practical exam (Foundation I & II together) is separate.

**Mock tests in this pack**

- **University paper (75 marks, 3 hours)** in the pattern above, drawn from the Foundation II questions and the first-aid questions here. For full practice, also answer a few Foundation I questions from that pack.
- **Quick MCQ test**: 20 questions in 20 minutes, for daily revision.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a favourite; comes up in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus hours and the usual style of B.Sc Nursing fundamentals papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Methods of physical examination, preparation of the patient, health history, abdominal examination order |
| 2 | Steps of the nursing process, nursing diagnosis (types, PES), goals, medical vs nursing diagnosis, a care plan; Orem and Roy |
| 3 | Nasogastric tube feeding, bed bath, pressure ulcers (causes, stages, Braden/Norton, prevention), oral care of the unconscious |
| 4 | Catheterisation and catheter care, enema, colostomy care, specimen collection, normal lab values, phases of diagnostic testing |
| 5 | Oxygen therapy (devices and precautions), suctioning, chest physiotherapy, chest drainage, pulse oximetry, incentive spirometry |
| 6 | Fluid volume deficit and excess, IV fluids and complications, drip-rate calculation, blood transfusion and reactions, intake–output |
| 7 | 10 rights, IM sites, dose calculation, medication errors, types of orders, storage, eye/ear drops, needle-stick injury |
| 8 | Care of the unconscious patient, Glasgow Coma Scale, stages of grief, care of the dying, last office, brain death |
| 9 | General Adaptation Syndrome, stress management, components of self-concept, body image, transcultural nursing, spiritual distress |
| 10 | CPR, choking, bleeding and shock, fractures, burns (Rule of Nines, first aid), snake bite, poisoning, transport of the injured |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Write procedures as numbered steps with a reason for each** — "Position the patient in left lateral — the rectum and sigmoid colon lie on the left, so fluid flows in by gravity." Examiners give marks for the rationale as much as for the step.
2. Organise long procedure answers under: **definition → purposes/indications → contraindications → equipment → preparation of patient → steps with rationale → after-care → complications → recording and reporting**.
3. For **situation-type essays** ("Mr X, 65 years, admitted with…"), use the nursing process: assessment findings, two or three nursing diagnoses in PES form, goals, interventions with rationale, evaluation.
4. Learn the numbers examiners like: GCS 3–15 (≤ 8 coma); Braden 6–23 (≤ 18 at risk); Norton 5–20 (≤ 14 at risk); SpO2 95–100%; Na+ 135–145 and K+ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L; pH 7.35–7.45; urine 1–2 L a day; injection angles ID 10–15°, SC 45°, IM 90°; CPR 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, 30:2; burns cooled for 20 minutes.
5. **Show every calculation** with the formula, units and answer — even a correct number without working may lose marks.
6. Use tables for comparisons: medical vs nursing diagnosis, types of interventions, IV fluid types, transfusion reactions, stages of grief, IM sites.
7. Very short answers (2 marks): one clear definition plus one example or fact.
8. MCQs come from small facts and safety rules; read every "Remember" list the night before.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour: write out the **steps of NG tube feeding, catheterisation, enema and IM injection with reasons** once each, do the drip-rate and dose-calculation formulas twice, draw the GCS table and the Rule of Nines, and then read the tables below.

**Assessment and nursing process**

| Item | Key fact |
| --- | --- |
| Examination methods | Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, olfaction; abdomen: inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate |
| Percussion notes | Resonant lung; hyper-resonant emphysema; tympanic stomach; dull liver; flat muscle |
| Stethoscope | Diaphragm high-pitched; bell low-pitched |
| Apex beat | Left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line |
| Nursing process | Assessment → Diagnosis → Planning → Implementation → Evaluation (ADPIE), cyclic |
| Diagnosis | PES: Problem, Etiology ("related to"), Signs ("as evidenced by"); types: problem-focused, risk, health promotion, syndrome |
| Goals | SMART; short-term and long-term |
| Interventions | Independent, dependent, collaborative; care direct and indirect |
| Theories | Nightingale environment; Orem self-care deficit (wholly compensatory, partly compensatory, supportive-educative); Roy adaptation (physiological, self-concept, role function, interdependence) |

**Basic needs and procedures**

| Topic | Must-know |
| --- | --- |
| BMI (Asian) | 18.5–22.9 normal, 23–24.9 overweight, ≥ 25 obese |
| NG tube | Length nose–earlobe–xiphisternum; confirm by aspirate pH ≤ 5.5 or X-ray; feed upright 30–45°, flush before and after |
| TPN | Central line, asepsis, pump, monitor glucose, do not stop suddenly |
| Pressure ulcer | Stages 1–4 + unstageable + deep tissue; Braden 6–23 (≤ 18 risk); Norton 5–20 (≤ 14 risk); turn 2-hourly |
| Perineal care | Front to back; replace foreskin |
| Urine | 1–2 L/day; oliguria < 400 mL; anuria < 100 mL; SG 1.005–1.030 |
| Catheter | Asepsis; female 5–7.5 cm, male 17–22 cm; inflate balloon after urine flows; bag below bladder; closed system |
| Enema | Left lateral; ~40 °C; can 30–45 cm high; tube 7.5–10 cm |
| Stoma | Pink-red and moist = healthy; flange 2–3 mm larger |
| Lab values | Hb M 13–17, F 12–15 g/dL; WBC 4,000–11,000; platelets 1.5–4.5 lakh; FBS 70–99 mg/dL; HbA1c ≥ 6.5% diabetes |
| Specimens | Midstream sterile; catheter sample from port; 24-h urine — discard first, keep last; sputum early morning before antibiotics |

**Oxygen and fluids**

| Topic | Must-know |
| --- | --- |
| SpO2 | 95–100% normal; accuracy falls with poor circulation, movement, nail polish, CO poisoning |
| Oxygen devices | Cannula 1–6 L/min; simple mask ≥ 5 L/min; Venturi fixed %; non-rebreather 10–15 L/min |
| Oxygen safety | Prescribed, humidified, no smoking or flames, no oil/grease |
| Suction | Only on withdrawal, 10–15 s per pass, pre-oxygenate |
| Chest drain | Bottle below chest, tube under water, tidalling, do not clamp routinely |
| Electrolytes | Na 135–145; K 3.5–5.0 mEq/L; pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO2 35–45; HCO3 22–26 |
| ROME | Respiratory opposite, Metabolic equal |
| IV fluids | Isotonic NS, RL; hypotonic 0.45% NaCl; hypertonic 3% NaCl, D10, DNS |
| Drip rate | drops/min = volume × drop factor ÷ minutes; mL/h = volume ÷ hours |
| Air embolism | Clamp, left side head down, oxygen |
| Blood | Two-person check; NS only; slow for 15 min and stay; reaction → stop, keep vein open with NS through new set, inform |

**Medicines**

```text
Amount to give = (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity    (same units first)
1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 µg; 1 L = 1,000 mL; 1% = 1 g in 100 mL
Example (invented): want 150 mg, have 250 mg in 5 mL → 150/250 × 5 = 3 mL
```

- 10 rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, education, refusal, assessment, evaluation; three label checks.
- Angles: ID 10–15°, SC 45°, IM 90°; ventrogluteal preferred, vastus lateralis infants, deltoid small volumes, avoid dorsogluteal (sciatic nerve).
- Z-track for irritant IM drugs. Never recap. White container for sharps; red for contaminated plastics; yellow for soiled and anatomical waste; blue for glass.
- Needle-stick: bleed freely, wash with soap and water, report, PEP ideally within 2 h, not after 72 h.
- Eye drops — lower sac; ear drops — adult pinna up and back, child < 3 down and back.
- Controlled drugs double-locked with a register; vaccines and insulin 2–8 °C.

**Sensory, dying, psychosocial**

| Topic | Must-know |
| --- | --- |
| Sensory | Reception → perception → reaction; deficit, deprivation, overload, poverty |
| GCS | E4 V5 M6 = 15; ≤ 8 coma; fall of 2 = urgent |
| Unconscious care | Lateral position, nothing by mouth, eyes protected, turn 2-hourly, talk to patient |
| Kübler-Ross | Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance |
| Rando | Recognise, react, recollect, relinquish, readjust, reinvest |
| After death | Algor (cooling), livor (pooling), rigor (stiffening) — last office before rigor |
| Euthanasia | Active illegal in India; passive and living wills only under Supreme Court guidelines (2011, 2018) |
| Self-concept | Personal identity, body image, role performance, self-esteem |
| Stress (Selye) | GAS: alarm → resistance → exhaustion; LAS: reflex pain, inflammation |
| Culture | Leininger transcultural nursing (Sunrise model); acculturation vs assimilation |

**First aid**

| Emergency | Do |
| --- | --- |
| Collapse | DR CAB; CPR 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, 30:2 or hands-only; AED |
| Choking adult | 5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts; infant 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts |
| Bleeding | Firm direct pressure; tourniquet only for life-threatening limb bleeding |
| Shock | Lie flat, legs raised (no injury), warm, nothing by mouth |
| Fracture | Immobilise joints above and below; RICE for sprains |
| Burns | Cool running water ≥ 20 min, cling film, no ice/oil/toothpaste; Rule of Nines (head 9, arm 9, front 18, back 18, leg 18, perineum 1) |
| Poisoning | No vomiting; keep container; hospital |
| Snake bite | Reassure, immobilise, hospital; no tourniquet, cut or suck |
| Dog bite | Soap and running water 15 min; anti-rabies vaccination |
| Heat stroke | Rapid cooling, call 112/108 |
| Triage | Red immediate, yellow delayed, green minor, black dead/expectant |

# Unit 1: Health assessment

INC Unit I (20 hours theory + 20 hours skill lab, taught with the mandatory 40-hour Health Assessment Module): interview and observation techniques, purposes and process of health assessment, health history, methods of physical examination, preparing the patient and the unit, general and system-wise assessment, and documenting the findings.

## 1.1 What health assessment is

**Health assessment** is the systematic collection of information about a person's health status — physical, psychological, social and spiritual — through a health history and a physical examination. It is the first and most important step of the nursing process: every nursing diagnosis, plan and evaluation depends on how carefully the nurse assessed.

**Purposes**

1. To collect baseline data against which later changes are compared.
2. To identify actual and potential health problems and the patient's strengths.
3. To make nursing diagnoses and plan individual care.
4. To evaluate the response to care and treatment.
5. To detect early warning signs (for example a falling level of consciousness) and report them.
6. To screen healthy people (school health, antenatal, occupational check-ups) and promote health.
7. To build a trusting nurse–patient relationship through the interview.

**Types of assessment**

| Type | When | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comprehensive (initial) | On admission | Full history and head-to-toe examination |
| Focused (problem-oriented) | For one complaint | Chest assessment in a breathless patient |
| Ongoing (follow-up) | At set intervals | Hourly vital signs and wound check after surgery |
| Emergency | Life threat | Rapid airway, breathing, circulation check |

## 1.2 Interview techniques

The **interview** is a planned, purposeful conversation to obtain the health history.

**Phases of the interview**

1. **Preparatory (pre-interaction)**: read the records, plan the questions, choose a quiet private place and a time when the patient is comfortable.
2. **Introduction (orientation)**: greet the patient by name, introduce yourself, explain the purpose and how long it will take, assure confidentiality, get consent.
3. **Working phase**: collect the history using the techniques below.
4. **Termination**: summarise, ask "Is there anything else you want to tell me?", thank the patient and explain what happens next.

**Communication techniques used**

| Technique | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Open-ended questions | "Tell me about your pain." — gives a full picture in the patient's words |
| Closed questions | "Do you smoke?" — quick facts, yes/no answers |
| Clarification | "What do you mean by 'giddy'?" |
| Reflection | Repeating the feeling back: "You seem worried about the operation." |
| Paraphrasing and summarising | Checks that you have understood |
| Silence | Gives time to think and express feelings |
| Active listening | Eye contact (as culture allows), nodding, not interrupting |

Avoid leading questions ("You don't drink, do you?"), medical jargon, rushing, and giving false reassurance. Use an interpreter when the language differs, and take history from a relative (secondary source) when the patient cannot speak.

## 1.3 Observation techniques

**Observation** means gathering data with all the senses — looking, listening, touching and smelling — from the first contact. Observe:

- **General appearance**: build, posture, gait, grooming, facial expression, distress.
- **Behaviour and mood**: anxious, restless, withdrawn, confused.
- **Environment**: bedside articles, drains, IV lines, oxygen, smell in the room.
- **Non-verbal cues**: grimacing, guarding a part, clutching the chest.

Good observation is objective: describe what you saw ("patient holding the right lower abdomen, knees drawn up") rather than a judgement ("patient is dramatic").

## 1.4 The process of health assessment

```text
Prepare → Health history (subjective data) → Physical examination (objective data)
→ Review of records and test results → Organise and validate → Document and report
```

- **Subjective data**: what the patient says (symptoms such as pain, nausea, worry). Recorded in the patient's words where possible.
- **Objective data**: what the nurse observes or measures (pulse 110/min, wound discharge, Hb 9 g/dL).

## 1.5 The health history

| Part | What it includes |
| --- | --- |
| Biographic (demographic) data | Name, age, sex, address, religion, education, occupation, income, marital status, informant |
| Chief complaint | Main reason for seeking care, in the patient's words, with duration |
| History of present illness | Onset, location, duration, character, aggravating and relieving factors, associated symptoms, treatment taken (memory aid: OLDCART or PQRST for pain) |
| Past history | Earlier illnesses, operations, injuries, hospital stays, allergies, immunisations, blood transfusions |
| Family history | Diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, cancer, tuberculosis, mental illness, genetic disorders (a genogram helps) |
| Personal and lifestyle history | Diet, sleep, elimination, exercise, tobacco, alcohol and other substance use, hygiene |
| Socio-economic and environmental | Housing, water supply, sanitation, family support |
| Psychological and spiritual | Coping, stress, beliefs and practices that affect care |
| Menstrual and obstetric (women) | Menarche, cycle, LMP, gravida, para |
| Review of systems | Questions system by system from head to toe |

**PQRST for a symptom such as pain**: **P**rovoking/palliating factors, **Q**uality, **R**egion and radiation, **S**everity (0–10 scale), **T**ime (onset, duration, frequency).

## 1.6 Methods of physical examination

### Inspection
Systematic looking: colour, shape, size, symmetry, movement, swelling, lesions. Done first, in good daylight or bright white light, with the part exposed and compared with the other side.

### Palpation
Using the hands to feel texture, temperature, moisture, tenderness, masses, pulsations and organ size.

- **Light palpation** (about 1 cm depth): surface tenderness, muscle guarding.
- **Deep palpation** (about 4 cm, can be bimanual): organs and masses.
- Fingertips feel fine detail; the back (dorsum) of the hand feels temperature; the palm (ulnar surface) feels vibration (for example vocal fremitus).
- Warm the hands, keep nails short, and palpate tender areas last.

### Percussion
Tapping the body surface to produce sound and judge the density of tissue underneath.

- **Direct**: tapping the surface with a finger (for example over the sinuses).
- **Indirect (mediate)**: the middle finger of the non-dominant hand is placed firmly on the skin and its middle phalanx is struck with the tip of the middle finger of the other hand, with a loose wrist movement.

| Percussion note | Over | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resonant | Normal lung | Air-filled tissue |
| Hyper-resonant | Emphysema, pneumothorax | Too much air |
| Tympanic | Stomach, gas-filled bowel | Hollow organ with air |
| Dull | Liver, full bladder, consolidated lung | Solid or fluid-filled |
| Flat | Muscle, bone, large effusion | Very dense tissue |

### Auscultation
Listening with a stethoscope to heart, lung and bowel sounds and to blood vessels (bruits).

- **Diaphragm** (flat side): high-pitched sounds — normal breath sounds, bowel sounds, normal heart sounds S1 and S2. Press firmly.
- **Bell** (cup side): low-pitched sounds — extra heart sounds (S3, S4), murmurs, bruits. Rest lightly.
- Listen directly on the skin, in a quiet room, with warm chest piece.

### Olfaction
Smell can give clues:

| Odour | Possible cause |
| --- | --- |
| Fruity (acetone) breath | Diabetic ketoacidosis |
| Ammonia-like breath or skin | Kidney failure (uraemia) |
| Musty breath | Liver failure |
| Foul-smelling wound | Infection, anaerobes |
| Alcohol | Recent drinking |
| Faecal-smelling vomitus | Intestinal obstruction |

## 1.7 Preparation for examination

**Preparation of the unit (environment)**: warm, well-lit, private room or screened bed; examination table or bed at working height; hand-washing facility.

**Equipment tray**: thermometer, sphygmomanometer, stethoscope, watch with seconds hand, weighing machine and height scale, measuring tape, torch (penlight), tongue depressor, otoscope and ophthalmoscope (where used), tuning fork, percussion (patellar) hammer, Snellen chart, cotton wisp and safety pin for sensation, gloves, lubricant, specimen containers, drapes, kidney tray, record forms.

**Preparation of the patient**

1. Explain the procedure and get consent — reduces anxiety and gains co-operation.
2. Ask the patient to empty the bladder (and give a urine sample if required) — a full bladder is uncomfortable and interferes with abdominal examination.
3. Provide a gown and expose only the part being examined — maintains dignity and warmth.
4. A female chaperone is present when a male examines a female patient (and as per policy) — protects patient and examiner.
5. Position according to the area examined.

| Position | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Sitting | Head, neck, back, chest, upper limbs |
| Supine | Abdomen, front of chest, breasts, peripheral pulses |
| Dorsal recumbent (supine, knees bent) | Abdomen (relaxes muscles), perineum |
| Lithotomy | Vaginal and perineal examination |
| Sims' (left lateral, upper knee drawn up) | Rectal and vaginal examination, enema |
| Prone | Back and spine, hip movement |
| Knee–chest (genupectoral) | Rectal examination |
| Standing | Gait, posture, hernia, varicose veins |

## 1.8 General assessment (general survey)

1. **Appearance**: apparent age compared with real age, distress, consciousness, nutrition, hygiene, dress.
2. **Body build and posture**; gait.
3. **Height, weight, BMI**, mid-upper-arm circumference if needed.
4. **Vital signs**: temperature, pulse, respiration, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and pain score.
5. **Signs of common general findings** — remember "**PICCLE**": **P**allor (lower palpebral conjunctiva, nail beds, palms), **I**cterus (sclera, under the tongue), **C**yanosis (central — tongue, lips; peripheral — nail beds), **C**lubbing (loss of the angle at the nail bed), **L**ymphadenopathy (neck, axilla, groin), **E**dema (pitting over the shin and ankle; sacrum in bed-bound patients).
6. **Mental status**: orientation to time, place and person, speech, mood, memory.

## 1.9 Assessment of each body system (head to toe)

### Skin, hair and nails
- Colour (pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, flushing), temperature, moisture, texture, turgor (pinch the skin over the sternum or forearm; slow return suggests dehydration), lesions, scars, pressure areas.
- Hair: distribution, lice, dandruff, hair loss. Nails: colour, clubbing, koilonychia (spoon nails in iron deficiency).

### Head and neck
- Skull shape, scalp, face symmetry (facial palsy).
- **Eyes**: eyelids, conjunctiva (pallor, redness), sclera (jaundice), pupils — size, shape, equality and reaction to light (**PERRLA**: pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation), eye movements, visual acuity with a Snellen chart.
- **Ears**: pinna, discharge, wax, hearing (whisper test; Rinne and Weber tests with a tuning fork).
- **Nose**: deviated septum, discharge, patency of each nostril, sinus tenderness.
- **Mouth and throat**: lips, gums, teeth, dentures, tongue (coating, dryness), tonsils, breath odour.
- **Neck**: range of movement, thyroid enlargement, lymph nodes, position of trachea (central), jugular venous distension.

### Chest and lungs
- **Inspection**: shape (barrel chest, pigeon chest), symmetry of movement, rate, rhythm and depth of breathing, use of accessory muscles.
- **Palpation**: chest expansion, tenderness, tactile (vocal) fremitus.
- **Percussion**: resonant over normal lung; dull over fluid or consolidation.
- **Auscultation**: vesicular (normal, over most of the lung), bronchial (over the trachea), bronchovesicular; added sounds — crackles (fluid in small airways), wheeze (narrowed airways), rhonchi, pleural rub.

### Heart and blood vessels
- Apex beat: normally in the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
- Auscultation areas:

```text
Aortic area      2nd right intercostal space, beside the sternum
Pulmonary area   2nd left intercostal space, beside the sternum
Erb's point      3rd left intercostal space, beside the sternum
Tricuspid area   4th–5th left intercostal space, lower left sternal border
Mitral area      5th left intercostal space, midclavicular line (apex)
```

- S1 ("lub") — closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves; S2 ("dub") — closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves. Murmurs and extra sounds are reported.
- Peripheral pulses (radial, brachial, carotid, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), capillary refill (normally under about 2 seconds), varicose veins, calf tenderness.

### Breasts and axillae
Inspect for symmetry, skin dimpling, nipple retraction or discharge; palpate each quadrant and the axillary tail; teach breast self-examination.

### Abdomen
Order is changed: **inspection → auscultation → percussion → palpation**, because touching or tapping first can change bowel sounds.

- Inspection: contour (flat, distended), umbilicus, scars, visible peristalsis, veins.
- Auscultation: bowel sounds in all four quadrants (normally about 5–30 irregular gurgles per minute; listen for up to five minutes before calling them absent); bruits over the aorta and renal arteries.
- Percussion: tympany over bowel, dullness over liver and full bladder; shifting dullness for fluid (ascites).
- Palpation: light, then deep; liver, spleen and kidneys; tenderness, rebound tenderness, masses, bladder distension.

```text
         Right Upper | Left Upper
        ------------ + ------------   (umbilicus at the centre)
         Right Lower | Left Lower
```

### Genito-urinary and rectal
Done with privacy, chaperone and consent; look for discharge, swelling, lesions, haemorrhoids; ask about urine and bowel habits.

### Musculoskeletal
Posture, gait, joint swelling, deformity, range of motion, muscle strength (graded 0–5), muscle wasting.

### Neurological
- Level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale — see Unit 8), orientation, memory, speech.
- Cranial nerves (simple tests such as smell, vision, eye movements, facial movement, hearing, swallowing, tongue movement).
- Motor: power, tone, coordination (finger–nose test).
- Sensory: touch, pain, temperature.
- Reflexes: biceps, triceps, knee jerk, ankle jerk, plantar response.

## 1.10 Documenting health assessment findings

- Record **promptly**, in ink or the electronic record, in the approved format (head-to-toe or system-wise).
- Write **facts, not opinions**; use measurements ("wound 3 cm × 2 cm, serous discharge").
- Use the patient's own words for subjective data, in quotation marks.
- Use only approved abbreviations; date, time and sign every entry.
- Record normal as well as abnormal findings ("breath sounds vesicular, no added sounds").
- Report abnormal findings (falling GCS, low SpO2, new chest pain) to the nurse in charge and doctor at once, and record that you reported.

## 1.11 Nursing points

- A good assessment is **systematic** (the same order each time), **complete**, **accurate**, **objective** and **respectful**.
- Always compare right and left sides.
- Be culturally sensitive: some patients prefer a nurse of the same sex.
- In the elderly allow more time, check hearing and vision first, and look carefully at skin and nutrition.
- In children, examine the least distressing parts first and leave the throat and ears till last.

## Remember

- Health assessment = health history (subjective) + physical examination (objective).
- Methods: inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, olfaction.
- Abdomen: inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation.
- Percussion notes: resonant (lung), hyper-resonant (excess air), tympanic (stomach), dull (liver), flat (muscle).
- Diaphragm of stethoscope for high-pitched sounds; bell for low-pitched sounds.
- Apex beat: left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
- PERRLA for pupils; PQRST for symptoms; PICCLE for general findings.
- Empty bladder, privacy, chaperone, warm hands, expose one part at a time.
- Document facts, measurements and the patient's words; report abnormal findings at once.

# Unit 2: The nursing process and introduction to nursing theories

INC Unit II (13 hours theory + 8 hours skill lab) — critical thinking and the five steps of the nursing process — joined with INC Unit XVI (6 hours) — meaning, purposes and types of nursing theories, with Nightingale, Orem and Roy. They are studied together because theories give the framework within which the nursing process is used.

## 2.1 Critical thinking in nursing

**Critical thinking** is purposeful, reasoned thinking: questioning information, looking at it from different angles, and reaching a sound judgement about what to do. In nursing it turns data into safe decisions.

**Critical thinking competencies**

1. **General critical thinking**: scientific method, problem solving, decision making.
2. **Specific critical thinking in clinical situations**: diagnostic reasoning, clinical inference, clinical decision making.
3. **Specific to nursing**: the nursing process.

**Attitudes for critical thinking**

| Attitude | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Confidence | Trusts own sound judgement, knows own limits |
| Independent thinking | Considers different ideas, does not just copy others |
| Fairness | Listens to all views without bias |
| Responsibility and authority | Follows standards and accepts accountability |
| Risk taking | Willing to question a doubtful order |
| Discipline | Thorough and systematic |
| Perseverance | Keeps looking for the answer to a difficult problem |
| Creativity | Finds new ways to meet a patient's needs |
| Curiosity | Asks "why?" |
| Integrity | Honest, admits mistakes |
| Humility | Recognises the need for more knowledge |

**Levels of critical thinking in nursing**

1. **Basic**: the learner follows rules and procedures exactly and trusts experts to have the right answer.
2. **Complex**: the nurse begins to analyse and weigh options, recognising that there may be more than one solution.
3. **Commitment**: the nurse chooses an action, takes responsibility for it and learns from its outcome.

## 2.2 Nursing process: overview

The **nursing process** is a systematic, scientific, problem-solving method used to give individualised, holistic care. It has five steps, remembered as **ADPIE**:

```text
      ┌──────────────► Assessment ──────────────┐
      │                                          ▼
  Evaluation                               Nursing Diagnosis
      ▲                                          │
      │                                          ▼
 Implementation ◄──────────────────────── Planning
        (cyclic and continuous — evaluation leads back to reassessment)
```

**Characteristics**: cyclic and dynamic, client-centred, goal-directed, systematic, interpersonal, universally applicable, based on critical thinking.

**Benefits**: individualised care, continuity, better communication in the team, legal record, patient participation, professional growth.

## 2.3 Step 1: Assessment

**Collection of data**

- **Types of data**: subjective (stated by the patient — "I feel dizzy") and objective (observed or measured — BP 90/60 mmHg).
- **Sources**: primary (the patient — the best source) and secondary (family, other health team members, records, investigation reports, literature).
- **Methods**: interview (nursing history), observation, physical examination, review of records and tests.

**Organising data**: grouping data into a framework — Maslow's hierarchy of needs, Gordon's functional health patterns, body systems or a nursing theory.

**Validating data**: double-checking that data are accurate and complete — re-measure an abnormal reading, compare subjective and objective data (a patient who says "no pain" but grimaces), ask another nurse.

**Documenting data**: record promptly and accurately, using the patient's words for subjective data.

## 2.4 Step 2: Nursing diagnosis

A **nursing diagnosis** is a clinical judgement about the person's (or family's or community's) response to actual or potential health problems or life processes; it is the basis for choosing nursing interventions for which the nurse is accountable (NANDA International).

**Identification**: analyse the data, find cues and patterns, identify **problems**, **risks** and **strengths**.

**Parts of a diagnostic statement (PES format)**

| Part | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P — Problem | NANDA-I diagnostic label | Acute pain |
| E — Etiology | Related factor ("related to") | related to surgical incision |
| S — Signs and symptoms | Defining characteristics ("as evidenced by") | as evidenced by pain score 7/10, grimacing, guarding of abdomen |

**Types of nursing diagnosis (NANDA-I)**

| Type | Statement | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem-focused (actual) | Three parts (P, E, S) | Impaired skin integrity related to immobility as evidenced by stage 2 sacral pressure injury |
| Risk | Two parts (problem + risk factors), no signs yet | Risk for infection related to indwelling urinary catheter |
| Health promotion | Readiness to improve | Readiness for enhanced nutrition |
| Syndrome | Cluster of diagnoses | Disuse syndrome |

**Guidelines for formulating a nursing diagnosis**

1. Write it in terms of the patient's response, not a medical diagnosis ("Ineffective airway clearance", not "pneumonia").
2. Use "related to" rather than "due to" or "caused by".
3. The etiology must be something nursing can change.
4. Do not write a legally risky statement ("related to nurse not turning the patient").
5. Do not write a nursing need, a test or an equipment problem as a diagnosis ("needs bed bath", "catheter blocked").
6. Do not repeat the same idea in both parts.
7. Use NANDA-approved labels where possible.

**Examples of NANDA-I approved diagnoses**: Ineffective breathing pattern, Impaired gas exchange, Deficient fluid volume, Excess fluid volume, Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements, Constipation, Urinary retention, Impaired physical mobility, Self-care deficit (bathing), Risk for falls, Anxiety, Disturbed sleep pattern, Deficient knowledge, Grieving.

**Medical diagnosis versus nursing diagnosis**

| Medical diagnosis | Nursing diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| Names a disease or disorder | Describes the person's response to the disease or situation |
| Made by the doctor | Made by the nurse |
| Stays the same while the disease is present | Changes as the patient's response changes |
| Treatment is medical (drugs, surgery) | Treatment is by nursing interventions |
| Example: Diabetes mellitus | Example: Risk for unstable blood glucose level related to lack of knowledge of diet |

## 2.5 Step 3: Planning

**Types of planning**

1. **Initial planning**: by the admitting nurse, after the first assessment.
2. **Ongoing planning**: done during each shift as new data come in.
3. **Discharge planning**: begins on admission; prepares patient and family for care at home.

**Establishing priorities**: rank problems so that the most urgent are dealt with first.

- **High**: threat to life (airway obstruction, bleeding, shock).
- **Medium**: not life-threatening but may cause harm (acute pain, immobility).
- **Low**: needs that can wait or need little support.
- Use Maslow (physiological needs first) and the **ABC** rule (airway, breathing, circulation), and consider the patient's own priorities.

**Establishing goals and expected outcomes**

- **Purposes**: give direction to care, are the yardstick for evaluation, motivate patient and nurse.
- **Types**: **short-term** (hours to days, usually within the hospital stay) and **long-term** (weeks to months, often after discharge).
- **Components of a goal/outcome statement**: **Subject** (the patient), **Verb** (measurable action — states, walks, demonstrates), **Conditions** (with the help of a walker), **Performance criteria** (how much, how well — 50 metres without breathlessness), **Target time** (by the third post-operative day).
- **Guidelines** — goals should be **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound; patient-centred, derived from the diagnosis, agreed with the patient.

Example: "The patient will walk 50 metres along the corridor with a walker, without breathlessness, by the third post-operative day."

**Types of nursing interventions**

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Independent | Nurse decides and acts on own judgement | Turning 2-hourly, health teaching, positioning |
| Dependent | Need a doctor's order | Giving medicines, IV fluids |
| Collaborative (interdependent) | With other team members | Chest physiotherapy with the physiotherapist, diet plan with the dietitian |

**Selecting interventions**: choose actions that are safe, evidence-based, acceptable to the patient, achievable with available resources, and directed at the etiology.

- **Protocols**: written plans for a particular situation (for example care after a cardiac catheterisation).
- **Standing orders**: a doctor's pre-signed orders the nurse may carry out in defined situations (for example in an ICU or a primary health centre).

**Nursing Intervention Classification (NIC)** is a standardised list of nursing actions (each with a label, definition and activities). **Nursing Outcome Classification (NOC)** is a standardised list of patient outcomes with measurement scales. With NANDA-I they give a common language (**NNN linkage**) for care plans and electronic records.

**Guidelines for writing a care plan**

1. Date and sign the plan.
2. Use standard medical terms and approved abbreviations.
3. Be specific — "turn 2-hourly from back to left side to right side".
4. Refer to procedure manuals instead of writing every step.
5. Make it individual and include the patient's preferences.
6. Include collaborative and discharge aspects.
7. Keep it current — revise as the patient changes.

**Format of a care plan**

| Assessment | Nursing diagnosis | Goal/expected outcome | Interventions | Rationale | Evaluation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "I feel breathless." RR 28/min, SpO2 91% on room air, crackles at bases | Impaired gas exchange related to fluid in alveoli as evidenced by SpO2 91% and breathlessness | SpO2 ≥ 95% and RR 16–20/min within 24 h | Fowler's position; oxygen as prescribed; deep breathing; monitor SpO2 hourly | Upright position lets the lungs expand; oxygen raises arterial oxygen | Goal partly met; continue plan |

## 2.6 Step 4: Implementation

**Process of implementing the plan of care**

1. **Reassess** the patient — the condition may have changed.
2. **Review and revise** the plan if needed.
3. **Organise resources** — equipment, staff, time, environment.
4. **Anticipate and prevent complications**.
5. **Implement** the interventions with skill and safety.
6. **Document and communicate**.

**Skills needed**: cognitive (knowledge, judgement), interpersonal (communication, teaching), technical (procedures).

**Types of care**

- **Direct care**: interventions carried out through contact with the patient — feeding, bathing, giving medicines, teaching, counselling, emergency measures.
- **Indirect care**: actions away from the patient but on the patient's behalf — co-ordinating with other departments, writing records, managing the environment, infection control, arranging referrals.

## 2.7 Step 5: Evaluation

**Evaluation process**

1. Identify the expected outcomes (from the plan).
2. Collect data about the patient's response.
3. Compare the response with the outcome: **met**, **partly met** or **not met**.
4. Relate the nursing actions to the outcome.
5. Draw conclusions: continue, modify or end the plan; reassess if the goal was not met (was the diagnosis wrong? was the goal unrealistic? were interventions not carried out?).

**Types of evaluation**: **structure** (setting, equipment, staff), **process** (how care was given), **outcome** (change in the patient).

**Documentation and reporting**: record the evaluation statement with the data ("Goal met: patient walked 50 m with walker without breathlessness on day 3"), and report changes at handover.

## 2.8 Nursing theories: introduction

**Meaning and definition**: a **theory** is a set of related concepts, definitions and statements that describe, explain, predict or prescribe a phenomenon. A **nursing theory** is an organised framework of concepts that explains what nursing is, what nurses do and why.

**The four metaparadigm concepts** found in every nursing theory: **person**, **environment**, **health** and **nursing**.

**Purposes of nursing theories**

1. Give a scientific base and identity to the profession.
2. Guide practice, education and research.
3. Help nurses describe, explain and predict patient responses.
4. Improve the quality and consistency of care and communication.

**Types of theories**

| Type | Scope | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grand theories | Broad, abstract, apply to all nursing | Orem's self-care deficit theory, Roy's adaptation model |
| Middle-range theories | Narrower, testable, a specific phenomenon | Peplau's interpersonal relations, Pender's health promotion model, Mishel's uncertainty in illness |
| Practice (situation-specific) theories | Very narrow, one clinical situation | A theory of pain relief after surgery |

They can also be grouped by purpose — **descriptive** (describe a phenomenon) and **prescriptive** (direct actions to achieve outcomes).

## 2.9 Selected nursing theories

### Florence Nightingale — Environmental theory
- Nursing is putting the patient in the best condition for nature to act upon him.
- Focus on the **environment**: fresh air (ventilation), light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, proper drainage and sanitation, pure water, diet, and observation of the patient.
- Use today: infection control, hand hygiene, ward ventilation, noise control, nutrition.

### Dorothea Orem — Self-care deficit theory
Three linked theories:

1. **Theory of self-care**: people perform activities to maintain life and health. Self-care requisites are **universal** (air, water, food, elimination, activity and rest, solitude and social interaction, prevention of hazards, normal functioning), **developmental** (needs at each life stage) and **health-deviation** (needs arising from illness or injury).
2. **Theory of self-care deficit**: nursing is needed when the demand for self-care is greater than the person's ability (self-care agency).
3. **Theory of nursing systems**:

| Nursing system | When | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wholly compensatory | Patient can do nothing | Unconscious patient |
| Partly compensatory | Nurse and patient share care | Post-operative patient who can wash face but not walk |
| Supportive-educative | Patient can do it with teaching and support | New diabetic learning self-monitoring |

### Sister Callista Roy — Adaptation model
- The person is an **adaptive system** responding to stimuli from the environment.
- **Stimuli**: **focal** (the immediate one — surgery), **contextual** (other factors present — noisy ward), **residual** (unclear past beliefs and experiences).
- **Coping mechanisms**: regulator (physiological) and cognator (thinking and emotion).
- **Four adaptive modes**: **physiological**, **self-concept**, **role function**, **interdependence**.
- The goal of nursing is to promote adaptation in all four modes.

## 2.10 Use of theories in nursing practice

- **Assessment** is organised by the theory (Orem: what self-care can the patient do? Roy: which mode shows ineffective response?).
- **Diagnosis and planning** are framed by its concepts.
- **Education**: curricula built on theory.
- **Research**: theories are tested and refined.
- **Administration**: nursing models shape policies and documentation.

## Remember

- Nursing process: Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation — cyclic, client-centred, goal-directed.
- Data: subjective/objective; sources primary/secondary; methods interview, observation, examination, records.
- PES = Problem, Etiology ("related to"), Signs and symptoms ("as evidenced by").
- NANDA-I types: problem-focused, risk, health promotion, syndrome.
- Goals: SMART; short-term and long-term; components subject, verb, condition, criteria, time.
- Interventions: independent, dependent, collaborative; care: direct and indirect.
- NIC = interventions; NOC = outcomes.
- Theories: grand, middle-range, practice; metaparadigm = person, environment, health, nursing.
- Nightingale = environment; Orem = self-care deficit, three nursing systems; Roy = adaptation, four modes.

# Unit 3: Nutritional needs and hygiene

INC Unit III (5 hours theory + 5 hours skill lab) — nutritional needs, special and therapeutic diets, care in dysphagia, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, and oral, enteral and parenteral feeding — joined with INC Unit IV (5 hours theory + 15 hours skill lab) — hygiene, care of skin, pressure points and pressure ulcers (Braden and Norton scales), perineal, oral, eye, ear and nose care and assistive devices.

## Part A: Nutritional needs

## 3.1 Importance of nutrition in patient care

Good nutrition promotes healing of wounds, resistance to infection, recovery of strength and normal growth. Poor nutrition delays healing, causes pressure ulcers, muscle wasting, anaemia and lowered immunity, and lengthens hospital stay. Many patients lose weight in hospital because of illness, fasting for tests, poor appetite and unappetising food — the nurse watches for this.

## 3.2 Factors affecting nutritional needs

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Age and growth | Infants, adolescents, pregnant and lactating women need more per kg |
| Activity and occupation | Heavy workers need more energy |
| Illness | Fever, burns, infection and surgery raise needs; illness lowers appetite |
| Medicines | Some reduce appetite or cause nausea; some alter absorption |
| Socio-economic status | Poverty limits food choice |
| Culture and religion | Vegetarianism, fasting days, food taboos |
| Psychological state | Depression and anxiety reduce or increase intake |
| Oral and swallowing problems | Missing teeth, ill-fitting dentures, sore mouth, dysphagia |
| Alcohol and tobacco | Poor intake, vitamin deficiency |

## 3.3 Assessment of nutritional status

1. **Diet history**: 24-hour recall, food frequency, likes and dislikes, food allergies, appetite, chewing and swallowing.
2. **Anthropometry**: weight, height, **BMI** = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². For Asian Indian adults the cut-offs commonly used are: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5–22.9 normal, 23–24.9 overweight, 25 or more obese. Mid-upper-arm circumference, skinfold thickness and waist circumference also help.
3. **Clinical signs**: hair (dry, easily pulled), eyes (Bitot's spots in vitamin A deficiency), lips and tongue (angular stomatitis, glossitis in B-vitamin deficiency), gums (bleeding), nails (spoon-shaped in iron deficiency), skin, oedema, muscle wasting.
4. **Biochemical**: haemoglobin, serum albumin, total protein, blood glucose, lipid profile.
5. **Screening tools**: for example the Mini Nutritional Assessment for older people and the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST).

## 3.4 Review of special and therapeutic diets

**Hospital diets by consistency**

| Diet | Contents | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear liquid | Water, clear soups, strained fruit juice, coconut water, tea without milk | First feeds after surgery, before some tests |
| Full liquid | Clear liquids plus milk, curd drinks, custard, strained thin porridge | Progression after clear liquids, mouth problems |
| Soft | Easy to chew: khichdi, dalia, idli, mashed vegetables, eggs, curd | After surgery, chewing difficulty, elderly |
| Regular (normal) | Normal balanced diet | Patients with no restriction |

**Therapeutic diets (review from Nutrition)**: diabetic (controlled carbohydrate, high fibre), low-salt (hypertension, heart failure, oedema), low-fat (gall bladder, heart disease), high-protein high-calorie (burns, tuberculosis, malnutrition), low-protein (some kidney failures), high-fibre (constipation), low-residue (before bowel surgery), bland (peptic ulcer), purine-restricted (gout).

## 3.5 Care of patients with feeding problems

**Dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing)**
- Get a swallowing assessment before giving oral food after a stroke.
- Sit the patient upright (90° if possible) during and for 30 minutes after meals — gravity helps food go down and reduces aspiration.
- Give food of the advised texture (thickened fluids, soft pureed food), small amounts, with the chin slightly tucked down while swallowing.
- Allow enough time; check the mouth for pocketed food after meals; keep suction ready.
- Watch for coughing, choking, wet voice — signs of aspiration.

**Anorexia (loss of appetite)**
- Find the cause (pain, nausea, depression, medicines, smell).
- Give small frequent meals, favourite foods (within the diet), attractive service.
- Oral care before meals; a clean, odour-free environment; avoid procedures at meal time.

**Nausea and vomiting**
- Position on the side or sitting up to prevent aspiration; keep a kidney tray and tissues ready.
- Remove smells; give mouth wash after vomiting.
- Give sips of clear fluids, then dry foods such as toast or biscuits.
- Record the amount, colour and content of vomitus (blood, bile, coffee-ground material) and intake–output; watch for dehydration.
- Give anti-emetics as prescribed.

## 3.6 Meeting nutritional needs

### Oral feeding (assisting a patient to eat)
1. Offer bedpan or urinal and hand-washing before meals.
2. Provide oral care, dentures, glasses and hearing aid.
3. Position upright; protect clothing with a napkin.
4. Check the tray matches the prescribed diet.
5. Sit at eye level; let the patient choose the order; give small amounts and do not hurry.
6. For a visually impaired person use the **clock method** to describe where food is on the plate.
7. Record the amount eaten and fluids taken.

### Enteral feeding: nasogastric (or orogastric) tube

**Indications**: unconscious patients, dysphagia, oral or neck surgery, severe weakness, anorexia, premature babies (orogastric). Also used for gastric decompression and lavage.

**Equipment**: NG tube (Ryles tube) of suitable size, water-soluble lubricant, gloves, 50 mL syringe, pH indicator strips, adhesive tape, stethoscope, glass of water, kidney tray, feed at room temperature, measuring jug, towel.

**Procedure for insertion (main steps with reasons)**

1. Check the order, identify the patient, explain and get consent — co-operation makes passage easier.
2. Position in high Fowler's with the head slightly flexed — opens the oesophagus and closes the airway.
3. Measure the length: tip of the **nose → earlobe → xiphisternum (NEX)** and mark it — places the tip in the stomach.
4. Lubricate the tip with water-soluble jelly — reduces friction; oil-based lubricant could cause lipid pneumonia if aspirated.
5. Insert through the clearer nostril along the floor of the nose; ask the patient to swallow (sips of water if allowed) as the tube passes the pharynx.
6. Stop and withdraw if the patient coughs, chokes, becomes cyanosed or cannot speak — the tube may be in the larynx.
7. **Check position**: aspirate stomach contents and test with pH paper (a pH of 5.5 or below suggests the stomach); chest X-ray confirms when aspirate cannot be obtained or as per policy. The air-whoosh test and bubbling in water are not reliable.
8. Secure the tube with tape to the nose; note the mark at the nostril.

**Procedure for feeding**

1. Position at least 30–45° upright; keep it during feeding and for 30–60 minutes after — prevents reflux and aspiration.
2. Check tube position before every feed.
3. Aspirate and note the residual volume; act as per policy if large.
4. Flush with water (about 30 mL for adults) before and after the feed and after medicines — keeps the tube patent.
5. Pour the feed into a barrel (without plunger) held about 30–45 cm above the stomach and let it flow by gravity slowly; never force.
6. Pinch the tube when refilling — prevents air entering.
7. Give oral and nasal care; record type and amount of feed.

**Complications**: aspiration, tube blockage or displacement, diarrhoea, nasal erosion, nausea, fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

### Other enteral feeds
- **Types of feeds**: blenderised home-made feeds (milk, dal, rice water, juices strained) and commercial formulas (standard, high-protein, disease-specific).
- **Methods**: bolus (intermittent by syringe), intermittent by gravity, continuous by pump.
- **Gastrostomy** (tube into the stomach through the abdominal wall, often by endoscopy — PEG) and **jejunostomy** (into the jejunum): for long-term feeding, oesophageal obstruction or high aspiration risk. Care: clean the stoma daily, rotate the external disc if advised, check for leakage and infection, flush before and after use.

### Parenteral nutrition: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)
- **Meaning**: giving all nutrients (glucose, amino acids, lipids, electrolytes, vitamins, trace elements) directly into a vein, usually a central venous catheter because the solution is concentrated.
- **Indications**: non-functioning gut (obstruction, severe pancreatitis, short bowel), severe burns, prolonged inability to eat.
- **Nursing care**: strict aseptic technique for the line; infuse by pump at a constant rate; do not use the TPN line for other drugs or blood; monitor blood glucose regularly (high sugar is common), weight, intake and output, electrolytes and signs of infection; never stop TPN suddenly (rebound low sugar) — follow orders.

## Part B: Hygiene

## 3.7 Factors influencing hygienic practice

Culture and religion, socio-economic status, personal preference, knowledge, body image, developmental stage, physical condition (weakness, paralysis, pain), mental state, and availability of water and facilities.

## 3.8 Hygienic care: indications, purposes and effects of neglect

**Indications**: dependent patients — bedridden, unconscious, paralysed, post-operative, elderly, very ill.

**Purposes**: cleanliness, removal of sweat and micro-organisms, stimulation of circulation, comfort and relaxation, prevention of pressure ulcers and infection, observation of the skin, self-esteem.

**Effects of neglected care**: body odour, skin infections, pressure ulcers, pediculosis, dental caries, gum disease, parotitis, eye and ear infections, urinary infection, poor self-image and social withdrawal.

## 3.9 Care of the skin

**Bed bath (sponge bath)** — main steps

1. Explain, provide privacy, close windows, room warm; bring all articles (basins, warm water, soap, towels, washcloths, clean linen and clothes, comb, lotion, laundry bag).
2. Offer bedpan or urinal first.
3. Keep the patient covered with a bath blanket; expose only the part being washed.
4. Wash, rinse and dry in order from **clean to dirty**: eyes (plain water, inner to outer canthus), face, neck, arms (long strokes from wrist towards the axilla — helps venous return), hands, chest, abdomen, legs, feet, then back, and lastly the perineum (with fresh water and gloves).
5. Change water when it is cool or dirty.
6. Give back massage, dress the patient, change linen, comb hair, trim nails if needed.
7. Observe and record skin condition (redness, rashes, pressure areas).

**Feet and nail care**: soak, clean between toes, dry well, cut fingernails curved and toenails straight across. People with diabetes and poor circulation need special care — no cutting of corns, no hot water bottles.

**Hair care**: daily combing; hair wash in bed with a Kelly's pad or improvised trough; protect eyes and ears with cotton.

**Pediculosis (head lice) treatment**: identify lice and nits; wear gloves and protective apron; apply the prescribed medicated lotion as directed; comb with a fine-toothed comb; repeat as directed; wash or boil linen and combs; examine contacts.

## 3.10 Care of pressure points and pressure ulcers

A **pressure ulcer (pressure injury)** is localised damage to the skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by pressure, or pressure combined with shear.

**Pressure points**: in supine — occiput, scapulae, elbows, sacrum and coccyx, heels; in lateral — ear, shoulder, greater trochanter, knee, malleolus; in sitting — ischial tuberosities.

**Causes and risk factors**: unrelieved pressure, shear (sliding down in bed), friction, moisture (sweat, incontinence), immobility, poor nutrition, anaemia, low albumin, oedema, reduced sensation, old age, unconsciousness.

**Stages (NPIAP classification)**

| Stage | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Intact skin with non-blanchable redness |
| Stage 2 | Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis; pink wound bed or intact/ruptured blister |
| Stage 3 | Full-thickness skin loss; fat visible; slough may be present |
| Stage 4 | Full-thickness skin and tissue loss with exposed fascia, muscle, tendon or bone |
| Unstageable | Base covered by slough or eschar, depth cannot be seen |
| Deep tissue pressure injury | Intact or non-intact skin with persistent deep red, maroon or purple discolouration |

**Assessment scales**

| Scale | Items | Score range | At risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Braden** | Sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition (each 1–4), friction and shear (1–3) | 6–23 | 18 or less; lower score = higher risk (12 or less = high risk) |
| **Norton** | Physical condition, mental condition, activity, mobility, incontinence (each 1–4) | 5–20 | 14 or less; lower score = higher risk |

**Prevention**

1. Assess risk on admission and regularly.
2. Change position at least 2-hourly (more often if at high risk); 30° tilted side-lying; keep the head of the bed as low as the condition allows to reduce shear.
3. Use pressure-relieving devices: alternating-pressure air mattress, water or foam mattress, pillows to keep heels off the bed. Avoid ring (donut) cushions — they press on the circulation around.
4. Keep skin clean and dry; manage incontinence; use barrier cream.
5. Lift, do not drag — use draw sheet.
6. Keep linen dry and free of wrinkles and crumbs.
7. Good nutrition and hydration with enough protein.
8. Gentle back care; do not massage reddened bony areas (it damages the tissue further).

**Care of an existing pressure ulcer**: relieve pressure on it completely; clean with normal saline; dress as prescribed (moist wound healing); remove dead tissue as ordered; treat infection; improve nutrition; measure and document size, depth, stage and discharge regularly.

## 3.11 Perineal and meatal care

Done for patients with catheters, after delivery or surgery, and incontinence.

- Use gloves, warm water or prescribed solution, cotton swabs.
- **Female**: separate the labia; clean from front to back (pubis to anus), one swab per stroke, centre first then sides — prevents carrying bowel organisms to the urethra.
- **Male**: retract the foreskin (if not circumcised), clean the glans in circular movement from the meatus outward, then **replace the foreskin** — prevents paraphimosis.
- **Meatal (catheter) care**: clean the meatus and the first few centimetres of the catheter away from the meatus.

## 3.12 Oral care

**Purposes**: keep the mouth clean and moist, prevent infection (stomatitis, parotitis), remove bad breath, improve appetite.

**Self-care patients**: brush twice daily, floss, rinse.

**Special oral care (dependent or unconscious patients)**
1. Position on the side with the head turned (or low semi-Fowler's if conscious) — fluids run out, preventing aspiration.
2. Place a towel and kidney tray under the chin.
3. Use a padded tongue depressor or bite block to keep the mouth open; never put your fingers between the teeth.
4. Clean teeth, gums, palate and tongue with moist swabs held in an artery forceps, one swab per stroke, from the back forward.
5. Use only small amounts of fluid; suction if needed; never pour water into an unconscious patient's mouth.
6. Apply lip moisturiser; inspect for sores, bleeding, thrush; record.

**Denture care**: remove (upper first) with gauze; clean over a basin lined with a towel or water (prevents breaking if dropped); store in a labelled container of water when out of the mouth.

## 3.13 Care of eyes, ears and nose and assistive devices

- **Eyes**: clean with sterile normal saline swabs, inner to outer canthus, one swab per wipe. In the unconscious, keep eyelids closed and moist (as prescribed) to prevent corneal damage.
- **Eye glasses**: clean with water and a soft cloth, store in a labelled case.
- **Contact lenses**: wash hands, remove (soft lenses pinched off the eye, hard lenses with the lid technique), store in the right solution in a labelled case. Never leave them in an unconscious patient's eyes.
- **Ears**: clean the outer ear with a washcloth; do not insert buds or pins into the canal.
- **Hearing aid**: switch off when removing, clean with a dry cloth, store in a labelled box, check the battery; keep dry.
- **Nose**: clean crusts with moist cotton swabs; in a patient with an NG tube, clean around the tube and change tape to prevent pressure sores.

## Remember

- BMI = kg ÷ m²; Asian cut-offs: 18.5–22.9 normal, 23–24.9 overweight, 25+ obese.
- Diets by consistency: clear liquid → full liquid → soft → regular.
- NG tube length = Nose–Earlobe–Xiphisternum; confirm by aspirate pH 5.5 or below (or X-ray), never the "whoosh" test.
- Feed upright (30–45°), flush before and after, keep upright 30–60 minutes after.
- TPN: central line, aseptic, pump, monitor glucose, do not stop suddenly.
- Bed bath: clean to dirty; long strokes towards the heart.
- Braden 6–23 (≤18 at risk); Norton 5–20 (≤14 at risk); low score = high risk.
- Turn 2-hourly; no ring cushions; do not massage reddened bony points.
- Perineal care front to back; replace the foreskin.
- Unconscious oral care: side-lying, moist swabs, no pouring of water.
