# Unit 4: Elimination needs and diagnostic testing

INC Unit V (10 hours theory + 10 hours skill lab) — urinary and bowel elimination, catheter care, enemas, suppositories, bowel wash, digital evacuation and ostomy care — joined with INC Unit VI (3 hours theory + 4 hours skill lab) — phases of diagnostic testing, common investigations with normal values, specimen collection and an overview of radiological and endoscopic procedures.

## Part A: Urinary elimination

## 4.1 Review: physiology and characteristics of urine

The kidneys filter blood, reabsorb what the body needs and excrete waste as urine. Urine passes through the ureters to the bladder. When about 200–400 mL collects, stretch receptors send signals to the spinal cord (S2–S4); the detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter relaxes; voluntary relaxation of the external sphincter allows **micturition**.

| Feature | Normal |
| --- | --- |
| Amount | About 1–2 litres a day in adults (about 0.5 mL/kg/hour or more) |
| Colour | Pale yellow to amber (from urochrome) |
| Clarity | Clear when fresh |
| Odour | Faintly aromatic; ammonia smell on standing |
| Reaction (pH) | Slightly acidic, average about 6 (range about 4.5–8) |
| Specific gravity | About 1.005–1.030 |
| Abnormal constituents | No glucose, protein, ketones, blood or pus cells |

## 4.2 Factors influencing urination

Fluid intake, diet (caffeine, alcohol increase urine), muscle tone, psychological factors (anxiety, lack of privacy), posture (men usually stand), age (enuresis in children, frequency in the elderly), pregnancy, surgery and anaesthesia, pain, medicines (diuretics increase, some sedatives cause retention), and diseases of kidney, bladder, prostate or nerves.

## 4.3 Alterations in urinary elimination

| Alteration | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Polyuria | Large volume (more than about 2.5–3 L a day) |
| Oliguria | Low output (less than about 400 mL a day) |
| Anuria | Almost no urine (less than about 100 mL a day) |
| Frequency | Voiding often in small amounts |
| Urgency | Sudden strong need to void |
| Dysuria | Painful or burning micturition |
| Nocturia | Waking at night to void |
| Haematuria | Blood in urine |
| Urinary retention | Bladder full but cannot empty |
| Enuresis | Involuntary voiding, often at night in children |
| Urinary incontinence | Loss of control: **stress** (with coughing, sneezing), **urge** (cannot hold after urge), **overflow** (dribbling from an over-full bladder), **functional** (cannot reach toilet in time — mobility or confusion), **reflex** (no sensation, as in spinal injury) |

**Nursing measures to help a patient void (before catheterising)**: privacy, normal position (sitting or standing if allowed), warm bedpan, sound of running water, pouring warm water over the perineum, warm drinks if allowed, relieving pain and anxiety. Catheterise only when these fail and it is ordered.

## 4.4 Facilitating urine elimination

### Providing a bedpan or urinal
1. Explain, screen, wash hands, wear gloves; warm the bedpan.
2. Ask the patient to raise the hips (or roll to the side, place the pan against the buttocks and roll back); place it with the broad end under the buttocks.
3. Raise the head end (unless contraindicated) — a more natural position.
4. Give toilet paper and the call bell; leave if safe.
5. Remove, clean the perineum front to back, offer hand washing, observe and measure the contents, clean the pan and record.

### Condom (external) catheter
For incontinent men with normal bladder emptying. Clean and dry the penis, roll the sheath on leaving 2–5 cm space at the tip, secure without being tight (risk of cutting off circulation), connect to a drainage bag, change daily and inspect the skin.

### Intermittent catheterisation
The bladder is drained with a straight catheter that is then removed — used for retention, residual urine measurement and sterile specimens, and as **clean intermittent self-catheterisation** in neurogenic bladder (spinal injury) at regular intervals. Lower infection rate than an indwelling catheter.

### Indwelling (retention) catheter — insertion

**Equipment**: sterile catheterisation tray, Foley catheter of the right size (commonly 14–16 Fr for adults), sterile gloves, antiseptic or cleansing solution, sterile lubricant (anaesthetic gel as prescribed for men), syringe with sterile water to inflate the balloon (amount printed on the catheter), closed drainage bag, drapes, light.

**Steps with reasons**

1. Check the order, identify, explain, consent, privacy — dignity and co-operation.
2. Position: female — dorsal recumbent with knees flexed and apart; male — supine with legs slightly apart.
3. Perineal cleaning with soap and water, then hand hygiene.
4. Open the tray; sterile gloves; drape; test the balloon (if policy); lubricate.
5. **Female**: separate the labia with the non-dominant hand (which now stays there), clean the meatus front to back with one swab per stroke, insert about 5–7.5 cm until urine flows, then a little further.
   **Male**: hold the penis upright at about 90° to straighten the urethra, retract the foreskin, clean in circles from the meatus outward, insert about 17–22 cm until urine flows, then advance to the bifurcation; replace the foreskin.
6. Inflate the balloon only after urine flows (inflating in the urethra causes injury); gently pull back until resistance is felt.
7. Connect to a closed drainage system; secure the catheter to the thigh (female) or lower abdomen/thigh (male) — prevents pulling on the bladder neck.
8. Hang the bag below bladder level, off the floor — prevents backflow and infection.
9. Record date, size, balloon volume, amount and nature of urine.

### Care of a patient with an indwelling catheter and urinary drainage
- Keep the drainage **closed** — do not disconnect.
- Bag below bladder level; empty when two-thirds full using a clean container for each patient; no kinks.
- Meatal care daily and after bowel movements.
- Encourage fluids (unless restricted) — flushes the bladder.
- Measure output; observe colour, clarity, sediment, blood.
- Take specimens from the sampling port with a sterile syringe after cleaning the port.
- Remove as soon as no longer needed — **catheter-associated urinary tract infection** risk rises each day.
- Removal: deflate the balloon fully with a syringe, withdraw gently, record the time, and check that the patient passes urine within about 6–8 hours.

### Urinary diversions
Surgical re-routing of urine when the bladder is removed or diseased — **ileal conduit** (ureters into a segment of ileum that opens as a stoma), **ureterostomy**, **nephrostomy** (tube from the kidney through the skin), **suprapubic catheter**. Care: clean, well-fitting appliance; protect the skin; urine will be continuous; watch stoma colour (pink-red, moist) and urine output; encourage fluids.

### Bladder irrigation
Washing the bladder with sterile solution through a catheter to remove clots, debris or to instil medicine as prescribed. **Continuous bladder irrigation** (common after prostate surgery) uses a three-way catheter: one channel for the balloon, one for inflow, one for outflow. Use strict asepsis; keep inflow running at the ordered rate; output must exceed inflow — **true urine = total output − irrigation fluid**; watch for clots, bladder spasm and blocked outflow.

## Part B: Bowel elimination

## 4.5 Review: physiology and characteristics of faeces

Peristalsis moves contents through the colon, where water is absorbed. Mass movements (often after meals — the gastrocolic reflex) carry faeces into the rectum; stretch causes the urge to defaecate; relaxation of the anal sphincters and abdominal straining (Valsalva manoeuvre) expel the stool.

**Normal faeces**: brown (stercobilin), formed and soft, about 100–200 g a day in adults on a mixed diet, characteristic odour. Frequency varies from about three times a day to three times a week. Colour changes: clay-coloured (bile obstruction), black tarry (upper GI bleeding or iron tablets), red streaks (lower bleeding, haemorrhoids), mucus or pus (inflammation).

## 4.6 Factors affecting bowel elimination
Age, diet (fibre), fluid intake, activity, privacy and routine, psychological factors, pain (haemorrhoids, surgery), pregnancy, medicines (opioids constipate; antibiotics may cause diarrhoea), surgery and anaesthesia, diagnostic tests (barium), and disease.

## 4.7 Alterations in bowel elimination
- **Constipation**: infrequent, hard, dry stools passed with difficulty.
- **Faecal impaction**: a hard mass that cannot be passed; liquid stool may leak around it.
- **Diarrhoea**: frequent loose watery stools — risk of dehydration and skin breakdown.
- **Faecal incontinence**: loss of control over passage of stool.
- **Flatulence**: excess gas causing distension and discomfort.
- **Haemorrhoids**: dilated veins in the anal canal.

The **Bristol Stool Chart** (types 1–7) helps describe stool form.

## 4.8 Facilitating bowel elimination

### Enemas
An **enema** is the introduction of fluid into the rectum and colon through the anus.

| Type | Purpose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleansing — large volume (tap water, normal saline) | Empty the bowel before surgery, tests; constipation | Normal saline is safest; tap water repeated many times can upset fluid balance |
| Cleansing — small volume, ready-made (hypertonic) | Constipation, bowel preparation | Draws water into the bowel |
| Retention (oil) | Softens hard stool; retained 30 minutes or more | Followed by a cleansing enema |
| Carminative | Relieves flatulence | |
| Medicated | Gives a drug as prescribed | |
| Return-flow (Harris flush) | Removes flatus | Fluid in and out repeatedly |

**Procedure: cleansing enema (main steps)**

1. Check the order, explain, privacy, keep a bedpan and commode ready.
2. Position in the **left lateral (Sims') position** with the right knee flexed — the sigmoid colon and rectum lie on the left, so fluid flows in by gravity.
3. Warm the solution to about body temperature or slightly above (around 40 °C, checked with a thermometer) — cold fluid causes cramps; hot fluid burns.
4. Lubricate the tip; expel air from the tubing.
5. Ask the patient to breathe slowly through the mouth (relaxes the sphincter); insert the tube gently towards the umbilicus about 7.5–10 cm in adults.
6. Raise the can about 30–45 cm above the anus — low height gives slow flow and less cramping.
7. Let fluid flow slowly; if cramps occur, lower the can or clamp briefly.
8. Remove the tube; ask the patient to hold the fluid for 5–15 minutes as tolerated.
9. Help to the toilet, commode or bedpan; observe and record the result.

**Contraindications**: suspected appendicitis or intestinal obstruction, recent rectal or bowel surgery (unless ordered), severe bleeding, some cardiac conditions; use care in the elderly and children.

### Suppository
A cone-shaped drug form that melts at body temperature.
1. Left lateral position; gloves; unwrap and lubricate the tip.
2. Ask the patient to breathe through the mouth.
3. Insert with the index finger, tapered end first, along the rectal wall beyond the internal sphincter (about a finger's length in adults, about 2–3 cm deeper than the sphincter); not into a mass of stool, because it must touch the mucosa.
4. Ask the patient to retain it for the time stated (often 15–30 minutes for laxative suppositories).

### Bowel wash
Repeated washing of the large bowel with fluid until the return is clear — before bowel surgery or investigations, or to remove poisons as ordered. Done with a rectal tube and funnel: fluid poured in by gravity, then the funnel lowered over a bucket to siphon it out. Record the amount in and out.

### Digital evacuation of impacted faeces
Removing hard faeces with a gloved, lubricated finger, done only with an order. Insert one finger, gently break up the mass and remove pieces. Stop if the patient becomes faint or the pulse falls — rectal stimulation can trigger the **vagal reflex** (bradycardia). Follow with an enema if ordered.

### Care of patients with ostomies (bowel diversions)
An **ostomy** is a surgical opening; the **stoma** is the part seen on the abdomen.

- **Colostomy**: opening of the colon; stool from formed (sigmoid) to semi-liquid (ascending).
- **Ileostomy**: opening of the ileum; liquid, continuous, enzyme-rich output that irritates the skin.
- **Temporary** (loop) or **permanent** (end).

**Care**
1. A healthy stoma is moist and pink-red; report a dark, purple or black stoma (poor blood supply).
2. Change the pouch when it leaks or as recommended; empty it when one-third to half full.
3. Clean the skin with warm water, dry; measure the stoma and cut the flange opening about 2–3 mm larger than the stoma — protects skin without pressing on the stoma.
4. Use skin barrier; watch for excoriation, prolapse, retraction, stenosis.
5. Diet: chew well; for ileostomy, plenty of fluids and salt as advised, avoid high-fibre foods that can block the stoma.
6. Teach self-care and support body image; refer to support groups.

## Part C: Diagnostic testing

## 4.9 Phases of diagnostic testing

| Phase | Nurse's role |
| --- | --- |
| **Pre-test** | Check the order and consent; explain the test; preparation (fasting, diet, bowel preparation, full or empty bladder); check allergies (iodine contrast), pregnancy, medicines; correct container and label |
| **Intra-test** | Position and support the patient; maintain asepsis; collect the specimen correctly; observe for reactions |
| **Post-test** | Label and send the specimen promptly with the request form; care of the puncture site; observe for complications; resume diet when allowed; record and report results, and tell the doctor about abnormal values |

## 4.10 Common investigations and their normal values

Laboratory ranges differ slightly between laboratories; always read the reference range printed on the report.

| Test | Approximate adult normal value | Clinical meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | Men 13–17 g/dL; women 12–15 g/dL | Low = anaemia |
| Total WBC count | 4,000–11,000 per mm³ | High = infection, leukaemia; low = marrow suppression |
| Platelets | 1.5–4.5 lakh per mm³ | Low = bleeding risk |
| Serum sodium | 135–145 mEq/L | Fluid and electrolyte status |
| Serum potassium | 3.5–5.0 mEq/L | Too high or too low affects the heart |
| Serum chloride | About 96–106 mEq/L | |
| Total bilirubin (LFT) | About 0.3–1.2 mg/dL | High = jaundice |
| ALT and AST (LFT) | Up to about 40 U/L (varies) | High = liver cell injury |
| Serum albumin | 3.5–5.0 g/dL | Low = malnutrition, liver or kidney disease |
| Total cholesterol | Desirable below 200 mg/dL | Heart disease risk |
| LDL cholesterol | Optimal below 100 mg/dL | "Bad" cholesterol |
| HDL cholesterol | Above 40 (men), above 50 (women) mg/dL | "Good" cholesterol |
| Triglycerides | Below 150 mg/dL | |
| Fasting blood glucose (AC) | 70–99 mg/dL; 126 or above on two occasions suggests diabetes | |
| 2-hour post-meal glucose (PC) | Below 140 mg/dL; 200 or above suggests diabetes | |
| HbA1c | Below 5.7%; 5.7–6.4% prediabetes; 6.5% or above diabetes | Average sugar over about 3 months |
| Serum creatinine | About 0.6–1.2 mg/dL | Kidney function |

### Monitoring capillary blood glucose (glucometer random blood sugar — GRBS)
1. Check the meter, strip code and expiry; explain.
2. Wash the patient's hands with warm water and dry (sugar on fingers gives a false high; warmth increases blood flow).
3. Use the side of the fingertip (fewer nerve endings than the pad); rotate sites.
4. Prick with a single-use lancet; wipe away the first drop if policy says so; apply the drop to the strip.
5. Press the site with cotton; read and record; dispose of the lancet in the sharps container.
6. Report values outside the ordered range; follow the sliding-scale order if one exists.

### Stool routine examination
Collect a small fresh sample (about the size of a walnut, or a few spoonfuls if liquid) in a clean, dry container with a spoon; avoid mixing with urine or water; send promptly (warm, fresh specimen for amoebae). Tests: ova and cysts, occult blood, colour, consistency, mucus.

### Urine testing
- **Routine specimen**: a fresh sample, preferably the first morning (concentrated) in a clean container.
- **Midstream clean-catch specimen** (for culture): clean the meatus, pass the first part into the toilet, collect the middle part in a **sterile** container without touching the inside, send within about an hour or refrigerate.
- **Catheter specimen**: from the sampling port with a sterile syringe — never from the bag.
- **Timed (24-hour) specimen**: discard the first void at the start time, collect all urine for 24 hours including the last void at the end, keep the container cool and with any preservative supplied, label times.
- **Reagent strip (dipstick) tests**: dip a fresh sample, remove excess, read each pad against the colour chart at the stated time — glucose, albumin (protein), acetone (ketones), pH, specific gravity, blood. Ketones suggest uncontrolled diabetes or starvation; albumin suggests kidney disease or pre-eclampsia.

### Sputum culture
Early morning specimen (secretions collect overnight), before antibiotics. Rinse mouth with water (not antiseptic), take deep breaths and cough from deep in the chest into a sterile container; sputum, not saliva. Send promptly. For tuberculosis, follow the programme's instructions on the number of samples.

## 4.11 Overview of radiological and endoscopic procedures

| Procedure | Purpose | Nursing points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plain X-ray | Bones, chest, abdomen | Remove metal objects; ask about pregnancy |
| Contrast studies (barium swallow, meal, enema; IVP) | Outline hollow organs | Fasting and bowel preparation as ordered; check allergy for iodine contrast; after barium, fluids and laxative to clear it (white stools) |
| Ultrasound | Organs, pregnancy | Abdomen — fasting; pelvis — full bladder |
| CT scan | Cross-section images | Contrast allergy and kidney function check; remain still |
| MRI | Soft tissues, brain, spine | No metal (pacemakers, implants, oxygen cylinders); claustrophobia; noisy |
| Endoscopy (gastroscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy, cystoscopy) | Look inside, biopsy | Consent; nil by mouth before upper endoscopy (usually 6–8 h); bowel preparation for colonoscopy; after upper GI endoscopy or bronchoscopy, nothing by mouth until the gag reflex returns; watch for bleeding, pain, perforation |

## Remember

- Normal urine 1–2 L/day; oliguria under 400 mL; anuria under 100 mL; SG 1.005–1.030.
- Try nursing measures before catheterising; catheterise with strict asepsis; inflate the balloon only after urine flows.
- Closed drainage, bag below bladder, remove early — prevents CAUTI.
- Bladder irrigation: true urine = output − irrigant.
- Enema: left lateral, fluid warm (about 40 °C), can 30–45 cm high, tube 7.5–10 cm.
- Digital evacuation can slow the heart (vagal reflex).
- Stoma healthy = moist and pink-red; flange 2–3 mm larger than the stoma.
- Diagnostic testing has pre-, intra- and post-test phases.
- Fasting glucose 70–99 mg/dL; HbA1c 6.5% or more = diabetes; K+ 3.5–5.0; Na+ 135–145 mEq/L.
- Midstream specimen in a sterile container; catheter specimen from the port, never the bag; sputum early morning before antibiotics.

# Unit 5: Oxygenation needs

INC Unit VII (11 hours theory + 10 hours skill lab): review of cardiovascular and respiratory physiology, factors and conditions affecting breathing, alterations in oxygenation, and nursing interventions — airway care, oxygen administration, suctioning, chest physiotherapy, chest drainage, pulse oximetry, and restorative care (hydration, humidification, coughing, breathing exercises, incentive spirometry).

## 5.1 Review of cardiovascular and respiratory physiology

Oxygenation depends on four processes working together:

```text
1. Ventilation       air moves in and out of the lungs
2. Diffusion         O2 and CO2 cross the alveolar–capillary membrane
3. Transport         O2 carried by haemoglobin (about 97%) and dissolved in plasma
4. Perfusion         the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the tissues
```

- **Ventilation** needs a clear airway, a working diaphragm and intercostal muscles, elastic lungs and **surfactant** (keeps alveoli open), and a normal respiratory centre (medulla and pons).
- **Control**: the main stimulus to breathe is a rise in CO2 (detected by central chemoreceptors); low oxygen is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies. In some people with long-standing CO2 retention, the low-oxygen drive becomes more important — high oxygen must then be given carefully as prescribed.
- **Diffusion** depends on the surface area and thickness of the membrane and the pressure difference of gases.
- **Transport**: each haemoglobin molecule carries up to four O2 molecules; anaemia reduces carrying capacity even when SpO2 is normal.
- **Cardiac output** = stroke volume × heart rate; a failing heart reduces delivery of oxygen.

Normal values: respiratory rate 12–20/min in adults; SpO2 95–100% (often 88–92% is the prescribed target in chronic CO2-retaining lung disease); arterial PaO2 about 80–100 mmHg; PaCO2 35–45 mmHg.

## 5.2 Factors affecting respiratory functioning

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Age | Infants have small airways; the elderly have stiffer chest walls and weaker cough |
| Environment | Altitude (less oxygen), pollution, heat, allergens |
| Lifestyle | Smoking damages cilia and airways; exercise improves capacity |
| Obesity, pregnancy | Limit diaphragm movement |
| Posture and immobility | Lying flat reduces lung expansion; secretions pool |
| Anxiety and pain | Rapid shallow breathing; post-operative pain stops deep breathing |
| Medicines | Opioids and sedatives depress breathing |
| Anaemia, heart disease | Reduce transport and perfusion |
| Nutrition | Weak respiratory muscles in malnutrition |

## 5.3 Alterations in respiratory functioning — conditions affecting

| Process | Conditions |
| --- | --- |
| **Airway** | Tongue falling back in unconscious patients, secretions, foreign body, asthma (bronchospasm), tumour, oedema of larynx |
| **Movement of air** | Weak or paralysed muscles (spinal injury, Guillain–Barré syndrome), chest injury, pain, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, obesity, CNS depression |
| **Diffusion** | Pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema (loss of surface area) |
| **Oxygen transport** | Anaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, low cardiac output, shock |

## 5.4 Alterations in oxygenation

- **Hypoxaemia**: low oxygen in arterial blood.
- **Hypoxia**: inadequate oxygen at the tissue level. Early signs — restlessness, anxiety, confusion, rapid pulse and breathing, raised BP; late signs — cyanosis, falling BP, slow pulse, drowsiness.
- **Cyanosis**: bluish colour of skin and mucous membranes; a late sign and may be absent in severe anaemia.
- **Hypercapnia**: raised CO2 — headache, flushing, drowsiness, confusion.
- **Hyperventilation, hypoventilation**.
- **Dyspnoea**: difficult breathing; **orthopnoea**: breathless when lying flat (relieved by sitting up — common in heart failure).
- **Breathing patterns**: tachypnoea, bradypnoea, apnoea, Cheyne–Stokes (cycles of deepening then shallowing breaths with apnoea — seen near death and in brain injury), Kussmaul (deep, rapid — metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis).

## 5.5 Nursing assessment for oxygenation
History of cough (dry or productive), sputum (amount, colour, blood), breathlessness (when it occurs, how many pillows), chest pain, smoking, occupation; inspection of rate, rhythm, depth, chest movement, accessory muscles, flaring of nostrils, clubbing, cyanosis; auscultation; SpO2; investigations (ABG, chest X-ray, sputum, pulmonary function tests).

## 5.6 Maintenance of a patent airway
- **Positioning**: Fowler's or semi-Fowler's for conscious breathless patients (lets the diaphragm descend); **lateral (recovery) position** for unconscious patients (tongue falls forward, secretions drain out).
- **Head-tilt chin-lift** (or **jaw thrust** if neck injury is suspected) opens the airway.
- **Airway adjuncts**: oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway — size from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw, only in unconscious patients without a gag reflex; nasopharyngeal airway.
- Suction of secretions, coughing and hydration.
- Advanced airways (endotracheal tube, tracheostomy) are cared for with suctioning, humidification, cuff care and stoma care.

## 5.7 Oxygen administration

Oxygen is a medicine: it is given **on prescription** (except in an emergency as per protocol), with flow rate or target saturation written.

**Indications**: hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, shock, heart attack with low saturation, carbon monoxide poisoning, during and after anaesthesia.

**Sources**: central (piped) supply, oxygen cylinders (in India, medical oxygen cylinders are black with a white shoulder), oxygen concentrators.

**Equipment**: flow meter, humidifier with sterile water (filled to the mark), delivery device, tubing, "No smoking" sign.

**Delivery devices (typical device ranges)**

| Device | Typical flow | Approximate oxygen delivered | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nasal cannula (prongs) | 1–6 L/min | About 24–44% | Comfortable, patient can eat and talk |
| Simple face mask | 5–10 L/min | About 40–60% | At least 5 L/min to flush exhaled CO2 |
| Venturi mask | Set by colour-coded valve | Fixed, precise (about 24–60%) | Preferred where an exact concentration is needed (chronic lung disease) |
| Non-rebreather mask (with reservoir bag) | 10–15 L/min | High (about 60–90%) | Bag must stay inflated |
| Partial rebreather mask | 6–10 L/min | About 40–70% | |
| Oxygen tent, hood, head box | Varies | | Children and infants |

**Procedure (nasal cannula/mask) — main steps with reasons**

1. Check the prescription; identify the patient; explain; place in semi-Fowler's.
2. Check SpO2, respiration and colour before starting — baseline.
3. Fill the humidifier with sterile water to the mark — dry oxygen dries and irritates the mucosa (humidification is especially needed at higher flows).
4. Connect the device and set the prescribed flow; check that oxygen is flowing.
5. Fit the prongs into the nostrils (curve downward) or the mask over the nose and mouth; adjust the elastic.
6. Pad the ears and cheeks — prevents pressure sores.
7. Recheck SpO2 and breathing; record time, device, flow and response.
8. Give mouth and nose care; check the humidifier water level, tubing for kinks.

**Safety precautions**
- No smoking, open flames, lighted lamps or sparks near oxygen — oxygen supports combustion.
- Avoid oil, grease or alcohol-based products near the equipment.
- Secure cylinders upright on a stand; keep away from heat; check the content before transport.
- Use cotton linen and avoid static electricity.
- Do not give more oxygen than prescribed; watch for **oxygen toxicity** (prolonged high concentrations) and, in premature infants, retinopathy of prematurity.

## 5.8 Suctioning

**Purpose**: remove secretions the patient cannot cough out, to keep the airway clear.

**Types**: oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal (clean technique), tracheal through an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy (sterile technique), open or closed (in-line) systems.

**Main steps with reasons**
1. Assess the need (gurgling, crackles, falling SpO2, visible secretions); explain; position semi-Fowler's (conscious) or lateral (unconscious).
2. Pre-oxygenate as prescribed (especially for tracheal suction) — suction removes oxygen too.
3. Check suction pressure — commonly about 100–150 mmHg for adults on wall suction (lower for children); higher pressure damages the mucosa.
4. Choose a catheter not wider than half the internal diameter of the tube; sterile gloves for tracheal suction.
5. Insert **without** applying suction; apply suction only while withdrawing with a rotating movement.
6. Limit each pass to about 10–15 seconds — longer passes cause hypoxia and bradycardia.
7. Let the patient rest and re-oxygenate between passes; maximum two to three passes.
8. Flush the tubing; observe and record amount, colour and consistency of secretions; check SpO2.

**Complications**: hypoxia, mucosal trauma and bleeding, infection, cardiac arrhythmias (vagal stimulation), raised intracranial pressure, laryngospasm.

## 5.9 Chest physiotherapy

Used to loosen and drain secretions — bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, lung abscess, patients unable to clear secretions.

- **Postural drainage**: positions that use gravity to drain particular lung segments (for example head down for lower lobes, sitting upright for upper lobes). Done before meals or at least 1–2 hours after meals (prevents vomiting); each position about 10–15 minutes as tolerated.
- **Percussion (clapping)**: striking the chest wall over the affected area with **cupped hands** to loosen secretions. Never over the spine, breastbone, kidneys, breasts, fractures or bare skin (use a towel).
- **Vibration**: a fine shaking pressure applied with flat hands while the patient breathes out slowly.
- Follow with coughing or suctioning.

**Contraindications**: unstable patients, haemoptysis, raised intracranial pressure, recent chest surgery or trauma, rib fractures, severe osteoporosis, bleeding disorders, pulmonary embolism.

## 5.10 Care of chest drainage

**Principles**: the pleural space normally has negative pressure that keeps the lungs expanded. Air (pneumothorax), fluid (effusion), blood (haemothorax) or pus (empyema) collapse the lung. A chest tube connected to an **underwater seal** lets air and fluid leave but not return.

**Purposes**: remove air, fluid or blood from the pleural space; re-expand the lung; restore negative pressure; after chest surgery.

```text
Chest tube ─► tubing ─► long tube under ~2 cm of water in the drainage bottle
                         (water acts as a one-way valve)
                         short tube open to air (or to suction as ordered)
```

**Nursing care**
1. Keep the drainage bottle **below the chest level** at all times — prevents backflow.
2. Check that the long tube stays under water; mark the fluid level and time.
3. Observe **tidalling** (water level rises and falls with breathing) — shows the system is patent; continuous bubbling in the water seal may mean an air leak.
4. Keep tubing free of kinks and loops; do not clamp routinely (clamping can cause tension pneumothorax) — clamp only as per policy, for example briefly when changing the bottle or if it breaks.
5. Keep two artery forceps (padded) at the bedside; if the tube disconnects, place the end in sterile water; if it comes out, cover the site with an occlusive dressing and call for help.
6. Encourage deep breathing and coughing; give pain relief as prescribed.
7. Record amount, colour and character of drainage; report sudden increase or bright red blood.

## 5.11 Pulse oximetry

A non-invasive method of measuring **oxygen saturation of haemoglobin (SpO2)** using red and infrared light passed through a finger, toe, earlobe or nose.

**Factors affecting accuracy**
- Poor peripheral circulation (cold, shock, vasoconstriction) — weak signal.
- Movement and shivering.
- Nail polish, artificial nails, dark-coloured dyes.
- Bright external light.
- Carbon monoxide poisoning (gives a falsely normal reading).
- Severe anaemia (the reading may look normal though oxygen content is low).
- Darker skin pigmentation can make readings overestimate saturation.
- Wrong probe size or position.

**Interpretation (adults, as a guide)**: 95–100% normal; 91–94% mild hypoxaemia; 90% or below needs urgent attention. Always look at the patient and the waveform/pulse reading together, not just the number. Rotate the probe site to avoid pressure injury.

## 5.12 Restorative and continuing care

- **Hydration**: adequate fluids (unless restricted) keep secretions thin and easy to cough out.
- **Humidification**: humidified oxygen, steam inhalation (with safety from burns), room humidifiers, nebulisation as prescribed.
- **Coughing techniques**:
  - *Deep cough*: sit upright, take a deep breath, hold for 2–3 seconds, cough forcefully twice.
  - *Huff coughing*: short forced breaths out with an open glottis ("huff") — less tiring.
  - *Splinting*: support an abdominal or chest incision with a pillow while coughing.
- **Breathing exercises**:
  - *Deep breathing*: slow breath in through the nose, hold, slow breath out through the mouth.
  - *Pursed-lip breathing*: breathe out slowly through lips pursed as if whistling — keeps airways open longer (chronic lung disease).
  - *Diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing*: hand on the abdomen should rise on breathing in.
- **Incentive spirometry**: a device that shows how deep a breath the patient takes, encouraging slow, sustained maximal inspiration. Sit upright, seal the lips around the mouthpiece, breathe in slowly to raise the ball or piston, hold for 3–5 seconds, breathe out; repeat about 10 times each hour while awake. Prevents atelectasis and pneumonia after surgery.
- **Positioning and early ambulation** improve lung expansion.

## Remember

- Oxygenation = ventilation + diffusion + transport + perfusion.
- Early hypoxia: restlessness, confusion, tachycardia; cyanosis is late.
- Orthopnoea = breathless lying flat; Kussmaul = deep rapid breathing of metabolic acidosis.
- Oxygen is a prescribed drug; humidify; no smoking or flames; Venturi mask gives a fixed concentration.
- Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min; simple mask at least 5 L/min; non-rebreather 10–15 L/min with bag inflated.
- Suction: apply only on withdrawal, 10–15 seconds per pass, pre-oxygenate, sterile for tracheal suction.
- Postural drainage before meals; percussion with cupped hands, never over spine or kidneys.
- Chest drain: bottle below chest, tube under water, watch tidalling, avoid routine clamping.
- SpO2 normally 95–100%; poor circulation, movement, nail polish, CO poisoning affect accuracy.
- Incentive spirometer: slow deep breath, hold 3–5 s, about 10 times an hour.

# Unit 6: Fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance, IV therapy and blood transfusion

INC Unit VIII (5 hours theory + 10 hours skill lab): review of how the body regulates fluids, electrolytes and acid–base balance; factors affecting them; fluid volume deficit and excess; electrolyte and acid–base imbalances; intravenous therapy (venipuncture sites, types of IV fluids, calculations, complications); intake–output measurement; blood and blood components; restricting and enhancing fluid intake.

## 6.1 Review: body fluids

- Water is about **60% of body weight** in a young adult man (less in women and the elderly, more — about 75–80% — in newborns).
- **Intracellular fluid (ICF)**: about two-thirds of body water.
- **Extracellular fluid (ECF)**: about one-third — interstitial fluid (around cells), intravascular fluid (plasma), and a small transcellular part (CSF, pleural, synovial, digestive juices).

```text
Total body water (≈ 60% of body weight)
├── ICF ≈ 2/3 (≈ 40% of body weight)
└── ECF ≈ 1/3 (≈ 20% of body weight)
    ├── Interstitial ≈ 15%
    └── Plasma ≈ 5%
```

**Movement of fluids and solutes**: diffusion (high to low concentration), osmosis (water moves towards higher solute concentration), filtration (pushed by hydrostatic pressure), active transport (needs energy — the sodium–potassium pump).

**Regulation of fluid balance**

| Mechanism | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Thirst | Triggered by raised plasma osmolality or low volume |
| Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) | From the posterior pituitary; kidneys keep water |
| Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system | Low BP/volume → aldosterone → kidneys keep sodium and water, lose potassium |
| Atrial natriuretic peptide | Released when the heart is stretched; increases loss of sodium and water |
| Kidneys | Final regulator of water and electrolytes |

**Normal daily intake and output (adult, approximate)**: intake about 2,500 mL (drinks about 1,500 mL, food about 750 mL, metabolism about 250 mL); output about 2,500 mL (urine about 1,500 mL, skin and lungs about 900 mL insensible loss, faeces about 100 mL).

## 6.2 Review: electrolytes

| Electrolyte | Main site | Approximate normal serum level | Key roles |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium (Na+) | ECF | 135–145 mEq/L | Water balance, nerve and muscle function |
| Potassium (K+) | ICF | 3.5–5.0 mEq/L | Heart rhythm, muscle contraction |
| Calcium (Ca2+) | ECF, bone | About 8.5–10.5 mg/dL | Bones, clotting, muscle and nerve |
| Magnesium (Mg2+) | ICF | About 1.5–2.5 mEq/L | Enzymes, nerve and muscle |
| Chloride (Cl–) | ECF | About 96–106 mEq/L | Follows sodium |
| Bicarbonate (HCO3–) | ECF | 22–26 mEq/L | Buffer for acid–base balance |
| Phosphate | ICF, bone | About 2.5–4.5 mg/dL | Bones, energy (ATP) |

## 6.3 Review: acid–base balance

Normal arterial **pH 7.35–7.45**. Regulation:
1. **Buffers** (immediate): bicarbonate–carbonic acid, phosphate and protein (haemoglobin) buffers.
2. **Lungs** (minutes): blow off or keep CO2 (CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3–).
3. **Kidneys** (hours to days): excrete H+ and reabsorb or make bicarbonate.

Arterial blood gas normals: pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO2 35–45 mmHg; HCO3– 22–26 mEq/L; PaO2 80–100 mmHg.

## 6.4 Factors affecting fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance

Age (infants and elderly at greater risk), body size and fat, environmental heat, diet and fluid intake, stress, illness (fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, kidney and heart failure, diabetes), surgery, medicines (diuretics, laxatives, steroids), and loss of fluid through drains, NG suction and wounds.

## 6.5 Disturbances in fluid volume

### Fluid volume deficit
- **Hypovolaemia**: loss of water and electrolytes together from the ECF (bleeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns).
- **Dehydration**: loss of water alone, so serum sodium rises (fever, too little intake, diabetes insipidus).

**Signs**: thirst, dry mouth and tongue, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes (and depressed fontanelle in infants), weight loss, low and concentrated urine (high specific gravity), rapid weak pulse, low BP and postural drop, flat neck veins, confusion; raised haematocrit and blood urea.

**Nursing care**: oral fluids (ORS for diarrhoea), IV fluids as prescribed, intake–output, daily weight at the same time with the same scale, vital signs, mouth care, safety (fall risk from postural hypotension).

### Fluid volume excess
- **Fluid overload (hypervolaemia)**: too much isotonic fluid in the ECF (heart failure, kidney failure, too much IV fluid).
- **Oedema**: excess fluid in the interstitial space (raised capillary pressure, low plasma protein, blocked lymph drainage, leaky capillaries).

**Signs**: weight gain, pitting oedema, distended neck veins, bounding pulse, raised BP, breathlessness, crackles in the lungs, low haematocrit.

**Nursing care**: fluid and salt restriction as ordered, diuretics as prescribed, semi-Fowler's position, intake–output and daily weight, skin care over oedematous areas, monitor breathing.

**Grading pitting oedema (common scale)**: press for a few seconds over the shin — 1+ (about 2 mm, disappears quickly) to 4+ (about 8 mm, lasts several minutes).

## 6.6 Electrolyte imbalances

| Imbalance | Common causes | Key signs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hyponatraemia** (Na below 135) | Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, excess water, SIADH | Headache, confusion, nausea, muscle cramps, seizures |
| **Hypernatraemia** (Na above 145) | Water loss, too little water, diabetes insipidus | Thirst, dry sticky mucosa, restlessness, fever, confusion |
| **Hypokalaemia** (K below 3.5) | Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, NG suction | Muscle weakness, leg cramps, decreased bowel sounds, arrhythmias, flat T waves |
| **Hyperkalaemia** (K above 5.0) | Kidney failure, crush injuries, burns, haemolysis | Muscle weakness, tall peaked T waves, dangerous arrhythmias, cardiac arrest |
| **Hypocalcaemia** | Removal of parathyroids, pancreatitis, vitamin D deficiency | Tingling around mouth and fingers, muscle spasms, **Chvostek's** and **Trousseau's** signs, tetany |
| **Hypercalcaemia** | Hyperparathyroidism, cancer of bone, immobility | Weakness, constipation, kidney stones, confusion |
| **Hypomagnesaemia** | Alcoholism, malnutrition, diarrhoea | Tremors, increased reflexes, arrhythmias |
| **Hypermagnesaemia** | Kidney failure, excess magnesium | Drowsiness, low reflexes, low BP, respiratory depression |

Nursing points: potassium is never given as an undiluted IV push — it is diluted and given by controlled infusion as prescribed; monitor ECG in severe potassium imbalance; watch urine output before potassium-containing fluids.

## 6.7 Acid–base imbalances

| Imbalance | pH | Primary change | Common causes | Signs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory acidosis | Low | PaCO2 raised | Hypoventilation: COPD, opioid overdose, chest injury | Drowsiness, headache, confusion |
| Respiratory alkalosis | High | PaCO2 low | Hyperventilation: anxiety, pain, high altitude | Light-headedness, tingling, carpopedal spasm |
| Metabolic acidosis | Low | HCO3– low | Diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, severe diarrhoea, lactic acidosis | Kussmaul breathing, headache, confusion |
| Metabolic alkalosis | High | HCO3– high | Vomiting, NG suction, excess antacids | Slow shallow breathing, muscle twitching, tetany |

**Memory aid — "ROME"**: in **R**espiratory problems the pH and PaCO2 move in **O**pposite directions; in **M**etabolic problems the pH and HCO3– move in the same (**E**qual) direction. The body **compensates** — lungs for metabolic problems, kidneys for respiratory problems.

## 6.8 Intravenous therapy

**Purposes**: replace fluid and electrolytes, give medicines and blood, provide nutrition, keep a vein open in emergencies.

### Peripheral venipuncture sites
- **Preferred**: veins of the forearm and back of the hand — cephalic, basilic, median antebrachial veins and dorsal metacarpal veins; start distally and move upward.
- **Antecubital fossa** (median cubital vein) — good for blood sampling and emergencies; avoid for long infusions (bending blocks the flow).
- **Avoid**: an arm with an AV fistula, the side of mastectomy with lymph node removal, paralysed limbs, areas of infection, phlebitis, oedema or bruising, legs in adults (risk of thrombosis).
- **Infants**: scalp, hand, foot veins.

**IV cannula sizes (common colour code)**

| Gauge | Colour | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 14 G | Orange | Rapid large-volume transfusion, trauma |
| 16 G | Grey | Trauma, surgery, rapid blood |
| 18 G | Green | Blood transfusion, surgery |
| 20 G | Pink | Most adult infusions |
| 22 G | Blue | Small veins, children, elderly |
| 24 G | Yellow | Infants, children, very fragile veins |
| 26 G | Violet | Neonates |

The larger the gauge number, the smaller the cannula.

**Main steps of cannulation**: check the order; explain; hand hygiene and gloves; apply a tourniquet 10–15 cm above the site; choose a vein; clean with antiseptic and let it dry; anchor the vein; insert bevel up at about 15–30° angle; look for flashback; lower the angle and advance the cannula off the needle; release the tourniquet; remove the needle and dispose in the sharps container; connect and flush; secure with a transparent dressing; label with date, time and gauge.

### Types of IV fluids

| Type | Examples | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Isotonic** (same osmolality as plasma) | 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline), Ringer's lactate, 5% dextrose (isotonic in the bag but behaves as free water once the glucose is used) | Expands ECF volume; used for blood loss, dehydration, maintenance |
| **Hypotonic** | 0.45% sodium chloride | Water moves into cells; used for cellular dehydration — avoid in raised intracranial pressure |
| **Hypertonic** | 3% sodium chloride, 10% dextrose, dextrose 5% in normal saline (DNS) | Draws water out of cells into vessels; watch for fluid overload |
| **Colloids** | Albumin, dextran, gelatin and starch solutions | Stay in the vessels and draw fluid in; volume expanders |

### Calculation for making an IV fluid plan

**1. Rate in mL per hour** = total volume (mL) ÷ total time (hours)

**2. Drops per minute** = volume (mL) × drop factor (drops/mL) ÷ time (minutes)

The **drop factor** is printed on the infusion-set packet — commonly 15 or 20 drops/mL for adult (macro-drip) sets and 60 drops/mL for paediatric micro-drip sets.

**Worked examples (made-up orders)**

- Order: 1,000 mL normal saline over 8 hours with a 20 drops/mL set.
  mL/hour = 1,000 ÷ 8 = **125 mL/h**.
  drops/min = 1,000 × 20 ÷ (8 × 60) = 20,000 ÷ 480 = 41.7 ≈ **42 drops/min**.
- Order: 500 mL over 4 hours with a 15 drops/mL set.
  drops/min = 500 × 15 ÷ 240 = 7,500 ÷ 240 = 31.25 ≈ **31 drops/min**.
- With a micro-drip set (60 drops/mL), drops per minute = mL per hour. Example: 50 mL/h = 50 micro-drops/min.
- Time to finish: 1,000 mL at 125 mL/h = 8 hours.
- A 24-hour plan: if 3 litres are ordered in 24 hours, give 1 litre every 8 hours (125 mL/h), labelling each bag with start time, rate and expected finish time.

### Complications of IV therapy

| Complication | Signs | Nursing action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Infiltration** (non-irritant fluid into tissue) | Swelling, coolness, pallor, slow flow | Stop, remove, elevate limb, restart at another site |
| **Extravasation** (irritant/vesicant drug into tissue) | Pain, burning, blistering, tissue damage | Stop, inform at once, follow the extravasation protocol |
| **Phlebitis** (vein inflammation) | Redness, warmth, pain, red streak along the vein | Remove cannula, warm compress as ordered, record using a phlebitis score; resite |
| **Thrombophlebitis** | Phlebitis with a clot — hard cord-like vein | Remove, report, do not flush |
| **Haematoma** | Bruising, swelling at site | Pressure, remove |
| **Local infection** | Pus, redness | Remove, swab culture, report |
| **Septicaemia** | Fever, chills, low BP | Report urgently; cultures |
| **Fluid overload (circulatory overload)** | Breathlessness, crackles, raised BP, distended neck veins | Slow the infusion, sit up, report |
| **Air embolism** | Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, low BP, cyanosis | Clamp the line, place on **left side with head down**, oxygen, call for help |
| **Speed shock** (drug given too fast) | Flushing, headache, chest tightness, collapse | Stop and report; prevent by correct rates |
| **Catheter embolism** | Piece of cannula lost | Tourniquet above site as advised, report |

**Prevention**: aseptic technique, change sites and dressings as per policy, check the site every hour (or as per policy), use the correct rate, label all lines, do not let air in, use pumps for drugs where needed.

## 6.9 Measuring fluid intake and output

**Intake**: oral fluids (including semi-solids that melt such as ice cream, jelly), tube feeds, IV fluids, blood, irrigation fluid that is not returned.
**Output**: urine, vomitus, diarrhoea, drainage from wounds, drains and NG tubes, bleeding; insensible loss is estimated.

Use a measuring jug and the 24-hour intake–output chart; know the volume of hospital cups and glasses; total every shift and every 24 hours; report output below about 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 30 mL/hour in an adult) or a large positive or negative balance.

## 6.10 Administering blood and blood components

**Components**: whole blood, packed red cells (anaemia, bleeding), platelet concentrate (low platelets), fresh frozen plasma (clotting factors), cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen, factor VIII), albumin.

**Before transfusion**
1. Valid prescription and **written informed consent**.
2. Correct sample for grouping and cross-matching, labelled at the bedside.
3. Baseline temperature, pulse, respiration, BP.
4. Wide-bore cannula (18–20 G for adults).
5. **Bedside check by two qualified persons**: patient's name, hospital number, blood group and Rh, bag number, expiry date, compatibility label against the request form and the patient's wristband.
6. Inspect the bag: no clots, discolouration, leaks or bubbles.

**During**
1. Use a **blood administration set with a filter**; prime with the blood or normal saline. Use **only normal saline** in the same line — dextrose causes clumping and haemolysis; calcium-containing fluids such as Ringer's lactate can cause clotting; never add medicines to blood.
2. Start slowly for the first 15 minutes and **stay with the patient** — most severe reactions appear early.
3. Check vital signs at the start, after 15 minutes, as per policy during, and at the end.
4. Complete a unit of red cells within the time limit in the policy (usually within 4 hours of removal from the refrigerator); do not warm blood except with an approved warmer.

**Transfusion reactions**

| Reaction | Signs |
| --- | --- |
| Acute haemolytic (ABO mismatch) | Fever, chills, back or loin pain, chest pain, low BP, dark urine, bleeding — can be fatal |
| Febrile non-haemolytic | Fever, chills |
| Allergic | Itching, urticaria, rarely anaphylaxis |
| Circulatory overload | Breathlessness, crackles, raised BP |
| Bacterial contamination | High fever, shock |
| Delayed (days later) | Jaundice, falling haemoglobin; infections |

**If a reaction occurs**: **stop the transfusion immediately**; keep the vein open with normal saline through a **new** set; inform the doctor and blood bank; check vital signs often; recheck the identification; send the blood bag, set and fresh blood and urine samples to the blood bank as per protocol; give treatment as ordered; document.

## 6.11 Restricting and enhancing fluid intake

**Restricting** (heart failure, kidney failure, SIADH): explain why; divide the allowed amount over the day (more during waking hours and with medicines); use small cups; offer ice chips (counted as fluid), frequent mouth care and lip moisturiser to relieve thirst; record accurately.

**Enhancing** (dehydration, fever, UTI, kidney stones, constipation): explain why; set hourly targets; offer preferred drinks within the diet; keep water within reach; offer fluids each time you visit; record intake.

## Remember

- Body water ≈ 60% of weight; ICF two-thirds, ECF one-third.
- Na+ 135–145; K+ 3.5–5.0 mEq/L; arterial pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO2 35–45 mmHg; HCO3– 22–26 mEq/L.
- Hypovolaemia: weak fast pulse, low BP, poor turgor, concentrated urine; overload: crackles, neck veins, weight gain.
- Potassium never as an IV push.
- ROME: respiratory — opposite; metabolic — equal.
- mL/h = volume ÷ hours; drops/min = volume × drop factor ÷ minutes.
- 1,000 mL in 8 h at 20 drops/mL ≈ 42 drops/min; micro-drip: drops/min = mL/h.
- Air embolism: clamp, left side head down, oxygen.
- Blood: two-person bedside check, normal saline only, start slow and stay 15 minutes, stop at once if a reaction occurs and keep the vein open with saline through a new set.

# Unit 7: Administration of medications

INC Unit IX (20 hours theory + 22 hours skill lab) — the largest unit: definitions, nomenclature, effects, forms, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; factors affecting drug action; medication orders; systems of measurement and dose calculation; the 10 rights; medication errors; routes; storage and nurse's responsibility; abbreviations; developmental considerations; oral, sublingual and buccal routes; parenteral routes, equipment, vials and ampoules, safe disposal and needle-stick prevention; topical, instillation, irrigation, spraying and inhalation; and other parenteral routes.

> All numbers in the calculation examples below are invented for practice. Real doses always come from the prescription and the drug reference used by your hospital.

## 7.1 Introduction and definitions

- **Medication (drug)**: a substance used to prevent, diagnose, treat or relieve disease, or to change a body function.
- **Administration of medication**: giving a prescribed medicine to a patient by the right route, at the right time, safely, and recording it.
- **Drug nomenclature**:
  - **Chemical name** — describes the chemical structure.
  - **Generic (non-proprietary) name** — the official name, used in prescriptions and pharmacopoeias (for example paracetamol).
  - **Trade (brand, proprietary) name** — given by the manufacturer; one generic drug may have many brands.
  - **Official name** — the name listed in the pharmacopoeia (Indian Pharmacopoeia).
- **Purposes of medication**: prevent (vaccines), diagnose (contrast media), treat or cure (antibiotics), relieve symptoms (analgesics), replace deficiencies (insulin, thyroxine), support life functions.

## 7.2 Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics

**Pharmacokinetics** — what the body does to the drug ("ADME"):

```text
Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism (mainly liver) → Excretion (mainly kidneys)
```

- **Absorption**: passage from the site of administration into the blood; affected by route, blood flow, solubility, food and stomach acidity. IV route has no absorption phase.
- **Distribution**: carried by the blood to tissues; affected by circulation, protein binding, blood–brain and placental barriers.
- **Metabolism (biotransformation)**: usually makes the drug inactive and water-soluble; reduced in liver disease, the very young and the old. Oral drugs pass through the liver first (**first-pass effect**), so some oral drugs lose much of their effect.
- **Excretion**: mainly in urine; also bile, faeces, lungs, sweat, breast milk. Kidney disease causes accumulation.
- Useful terms: **onset** (time to start acting), **peak**, **duration**, **half-life** (time for the blood level to fall by half), **therapeutic range**, **trough**.

**Pharmacodynamics** — what the drug does to the body: drugs act mainly by binding to **receptors** (agonists activate, antagonists block), by altering enzymes, by physical or chemical action (antacids neutralise acid), or by acting on ion channels.

## 7.3 Effects of drugs

| Effect | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Therapeutic | The intended effect |
| Side effect | Predictable unwanted effect at normal dose (drowsiness with antihistamines) |
| Adverse effect | Harmful, unintended effect needing action |
| Toxic effect | Harmful effect from accumulation or overdose |
| Allergic reaction | Immune response — rash, itching, up to anaphylaxis |
| Idiosyncratic | Unusual, unexpected response peculiar to the person |
| Tolerance | Larger amounts needed for the same effect |
| Dependence | Physical or psychological need for the drug |
| Cumulative effect | Drug builds up when it is given faster than it is removed |
| Drug interaction | One drug changes the effect of another (synergism, antagonism) |
| Iatrogenic | Disease caused by treatment |

## 7.4 Forms of medications

| Route | Forms |
| --- | --- |
| Oral | Tablets (plain, enteric-coated, sustained-release), capsules, caplets, lozenges, powders, syrups, elixirs, suspensions, emulsions |
| Topical | Ointments, creams, lotions, pastes, gels, powders, transdermal patches |
| Body cavities | Suppositories, pessaries, drops, sprays |
| Inhalation | Metered-dose inhalers, dry-powder inhalers, nebuliser solutions |
| Parenteral | Solutions and suspensions in ampoules, vials, prefilled syringes, infusion bags |

Enteric-coated and sustained-release tablets must **not be crushed or chewed**.

## 7.5 Factors influencing medication action

Age (infants and elderly: immature or slowed metabolism and excretion), body weight and composition, sex, genetics, pregnancy and breast-feeding, disease (liver, kidney, heart), psychological factors (placebo effect), diet and food–drug interactions, timing in relation to meals, route, environment (heat, cold), tolerance, and other drugs taken.

## 7.6 Medication orders and prescriptions

**Parts of a complete order**: patient's full name and identification; date and time written; drug name (generic preferred); dose; route; frequency/time; duration where relevant; prescriber's signature (and registration number on prescriptions).

**Types of orders**

| Type | Meaning | Example (made-up) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routine (standing) | Given regularly until stopped or for a set period | Drug A tablet, twice daily for 5 days |
| PRN (as needed) | Given when the patient needs it, within set limits | Analgesic when pain score is above 4 |
| Single (one-time) | Given once at a stated time | Before surgery |
| STAT | Given immediately, once | In an emergency |
| Verbal / telephone | Spoken orders — only in emergencies or as per policy | Write it down, **read it back**, and get it signed within the time set by policy |

Do not carry out an order that is incomplete, illegible or seems wrong — clarify with the prescriber first.

## 7.7 Systems of measurement

- **Metric system** (standard): weight — kilogram (kg), gram (g), milligram (mg), microgram (µg or mcg); volume — litre (L), millilitre (mL).
- **Household measures**: teaspoon (about 5 mL), tablespoon (about 15 mL), cup, glass — inaccurate; use an oral syringe or medicine cup for exact measurement.
- **Units**: biological activity, for example insulin and heparin (write "units" in full).
- **Milliequivalents (mEq)**: electrolytes.
- **Apothecary system** (grains, minims, drams): old, mostly out of use.

**Conversions to know**

| From | To |
| --- | --- |
| 1 kg | 1,000 g |
| 1 g | 1,000 mg |
| 1 mg | 1,000 µg |
| 1 L | 1,000 mL |
| 1 kg | about 2.2 lb |
| 1 mL of water | 1 g; 1 mL = 1 cc |

To change a large unit to a smaller one, **multiply** (0.5 g × 1,000 = 500 mg). To change a small unit to a larger one, **divide** (250 mg ÷ 1,000 = 0.25 g).

## 7.8 Medication dose calculation

**Basic formula**

```text
Amount to give = (Desired dose ÷ Dose on hand) × Quantity it comes in
              = (D ÷ H) × Q
```

Always convert to the **same units first**, then estimate whether the answer is sensible.

**Practice examples (invented drugs and numbers)**

1. *Tablets*: Ordered Drug X 500 mg. Available: 250 mg tablets.
   (500 ÷ 250) × 1 tablet = **2 tablets**.
2. *Liquids*: Ordered Drug Y 150 mg. Available: 250 mg in 5 mL.
   (150 ÷ 250) × 5 mL = **3 mL**.
3. *Different units*: Ordered Drug Z 0.2 g. Available: 100 mg per tablet.
   0.2 g = 200 mg → (200 ÷ 100) × 1 = **2 tablets**.
4. *Injection*: Ordered Drug P 40 mg. Available: 80 mg in 2 mL.
   (40 ÷ 80) × 2 mL = **1 mL**.
5. *Reconstitution*: a vial contains 1 g of powder; the label says add 4 mL diluent to make 5 mL in total. Concentration = 1,000 mg ÷ 5 mL = 200 mg/mL. Ordered 300 mg → 300 ÷ 200 = **1.5 mL**.
6. *Weight-based*: Ordered 5 mg per kg for a 12 kg child (made-up drug). 5 × 12 = 60 mg. Available 120 mg in 5 mL → (60 ÷ 120) × 5 = **2.5 mL**.
7. *Percentage solutions*: a 1% solution contains 1 g in 100 mL (10 mg/mL). Preparing 500 mL of a 2% lotion from pure solute needs 2 × 5 = 10 g (or 10 mL if liquid) made up to 500 mL.
8. *Ratio strength*: 1:1,000 means 1 g in 1,000 mL (1 mg/mL).
9. *Dilution from a stronger solution*: C1 × V1 = C2 × V2. To make 1,000 mL of a 1% solution from a 5% stock: V1 = (1 × 1,000) ÷ 5 = 200 mL of stock made up to 1,000 mL.

(For IV drip rates see Unit 6.)

Double-check high-alert drug calculations (insulin, heparin, potassium, opioids, paediatric doses) with a second nurse.

## 7.9 Principles and the 10 rights of medication administration

**General principles**: know the drug (action, usual range, side effects, nursing points); give only what you have prepared yourself; never give from an unlabelled container; check expiry; do not return a prepared medicine to the stock bottle; stay with the patient until an oral medicine is swallowed; maintain asepsis for parenteral routes; record immediately after giving, never before.

**The 10 rights**

1. **Right patient** — check two identifiers (name and hospital number/wristband); ask the patient to state their name.
2. **Right drug** — compare the label with the order **three times**: when taking it from storage, while preparing, and before giving (or returning the container).
3. **Right dose** — calculate carefully; double-check high-risk drugs.
4. **Right route** — and the right form for that route.
5. **Right time** — and frequency; give within the time window set by policy.
6. **Right documentation** — record after giving: drug, dose, route, time, site, signature.
7. **Right client education** — tell the patient what the drug is for and what to expect.
8. **Right to refuse** — explain the consequences, inform the prescriber, record the refusal.
9. **Right assessment** — check what is needed before giving (allergy history, pulse before a cardiac drug, BP before an antihypertensive, swallowing ability).
10. **Right evaluation** — check the response and side effects afterwards.

(Some books list "right reason" or "right response" in place of one of these.)

## 7.10 Errors in medication administration

**Types**: wrong patient, drug, dose, route, time or form; omission; giving a drug to which the patient is allergic; giving a drug twice; wrong rate of infusion; wrong preparation.

**Common causes**: illegible or incomplete orders, look-alike and sound-alike names, calculation errors, misread abbreviations, distractions and interruptions, workload and fatigue, failing to check identity, poor communication at handover.

**Prevention**: follow the rights and three checks; clarify doubtful orders; use generic names and approved abbreviations; avoid interruptions during medicine rounds; double-check high-alert drugs; separate look-alike drugs; know the drugs you give.

**What to do after an error**: check the patient immediately and take vital signs; inform the nurse in charge and the doctor at once; give any ordered treatment; record the facts in the patient's notes; complete an incident report as per hospital policy; never hide an error — reporting protects the patient and improves the system.

## 7.11 Routes of administration

| Route | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral | Safe, cheap, convenient, painless | Slow; first-pass loss; not for vomiting, unconscious or NPO patients; taste |
| Sublingual (under the tongue) / buccal (against the cheek) | Rapid absorption, avoids first-pass effect | Only for small amounts of suitable drugs; must not be swallowed |
| Topical (skin, mucous membrane) | Local effect, few systemic effects | Messy, may irritate |
| Inhalation | Rapid local action in lungs | Needs correct technique |
| Rectal / vaginal | When oral is not possible; local effect | Uncomfortable, irregular absorption |
| Intradermal | Small amount for tests (tuberculin, sensitivity tests) | Very small volume |
| Subcutaneous | Slow, steady absorption (insulin, heparin, some vaccines) | Small volumes; irritation |
| Intramuscular | Faster absorption than subcutaneous; larger volumes than SC | Pain, nerve injury, abscess |
| Intravenous | Immediate action, 100% availability, for large volumes | Irreversible once given; infection, phlebitis, speed shock |

## 7.12 Storage and maintenance of drugs; nurse's responsibility

- Store in a locked cupboard or trolley; keys with the nurse in charge.
- **Narcotics and psychotropic substances** (controlled under the NDPS Act, 1985) in a separate double-locked cupboard, with a register counted and signed at every shift change.
- Keep internal and external medicines on separate shelves; poisonous and high-alert drugs separate and labelled.
- Store as the label says: room temperature, cool place, **refrigerator at 2–8 °C** for vaccines, insulin and some injections (not in the freezer or door); protect light-sensitive drugs in amber containers.
- Check expiry dates; use the "first expiry, first out" rule; return expired or damaged drugs to the pharmacy.
- Never transfer drugs between containers or relabel them.
- Keep labels clean and readable; discard if unreadable.
- Keep the emergency (crash) trolley checked and stocked.
- Keep records of stock, indents and controlled drugs.

## 7.13 Terminologies and abbreviations used in orders

| Abbreviation | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| OD | Once a day |
| BD / BID | Twice a day |
| TDS / TID | Three times a day |
| QID / QDS | Four times a day |
| HS | At bedtime |
| AC | Before meals |
| PC | After meals |
| SOS / PRN | When needed |
| STAT | Immediately |
| NPO / NBM | Nothing by mouth |
| PO | By mouth |
| SL | Sublingual |
| IM, IV, SC, ID | Intramuscular, intravenous, subcutaneous, intradermal |
| q4h | Every 4 hours |
| Tab, Cap, Syr, Inj | Tablet, capsule, syrup, injection |
| Rx | Prescription |

**Error-prone forms to avoid**: "U" or "IU" (write "units"), "µg" handwritten (write "mcg"), a trailing zero (write 5 mg, not 5.0 mg) and a missing leading zero (write 0.5 mg, not .5 mg), "OD" when it might be read as "right eye".

## 7.14 Developmental considerations

- **Infants and children**: doses by weight or body surface area; use an oral syringe or dropper, give slowly into the side of the mouth; do not add medicine to a full bottle of milk (the baby may not finish it); involve parents; the vastus lateralis is the IM site of choice in infants; use age-appropriate explanations and praise.
- **Pregnancy and lactation**: many drugs cross the placenta or enter milk; check with the prescriber.
- **Older adults**: slower metabolism and excretion, many medicines at once (polypharmacy), memory problems, poor vision, swallowing difficulty, fragile skin and less muscle mass; use large-print labels, pill organisers, review medicines regularly, watch for falls and confusion.

## 7.15 Oral, sublingual and buccal administration

**Equipment**: medicine trolley, medication record, medicine cups, oral syringes, spoon, water, pill crusher (only when the drug may be crushed), straws, tissue.

**Procedure — main steps with reasons**
1. Hand hygiene; check the order against the medication record — avoids transcription errors.
2. Check allergies and any assessment needed (pulse, BP, swallowing).
3. Prepare one patient's medicines at a time; check the label three times; pour tablets into the cap and then the cup without touching them; pour liquids with the label towards the palm (keeps the label clean) and read the level at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
4. Identify the patient with two identifiers; explain.
5. Sit the patient up — eases swallowing and prevents aspiration.
6. Give with a full glass of water (unless restricted); stay until all are swallowed — the patient may otherwise hoard or discard them.
7. **Sublingual**: place under the tongue and let it dissolve — no swallowing, eating or drinking until it dissolves. **Buccal**: place between the cheek and gum, alternate cheeks.
8. Document immediately; observe the effect.

**Points**: do not give oral medicines to patients who are vomiting, unconscious, NPO or unable to swallow; give medicines through an NG tube only in liquid form or crushed if allowed, one at a time, flushing before, between and after.

## 7.16 Introduction to parenteral administration

| Route | Sites | Needle (adult guide) | Angle | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Intradermal (ID)** | Inner forearm, upper back, upper arm | 26–27 G, about 1 cm | 10–15° (almost flat), bevel up | Raise a small bleb (wheal); do not massage |
| **Subcutaneous (SC)** | Outer upper arm, abdomen (about 5 cm away from the umbilicus), front of thighs, upper back | 25–27 G, short | 45° (90° if enough fat or with a short pen needle) | Pinch the skin; rotate sites; do not massage after heparin or insulin |
| **Intramuscular (IM)** | **Ventrogluteal** (preferred for adults — no major nerves or vessels), **vastus lateralis** (preferred in infants), **deltoid** (small volumes, vaccines), dorsogluteal (avoided — risk of sciatic nerve injury) | 21–23 G, 2.5–4 cm depending on muscle and fat | 90° | Z-track technique for irritating drugs; small volume in deltoid |
| **Intravenous (IV)** | Veins of forearm and hand | Cannula 18–22 G | 15–30° for cannulation | Bolus, intermittent infusion or continuous infusion |

**Locating IM sites**
- **Ventrogluteal**: place the palm on the greater trochanter (left hand on the right hip), index finger on the anterior superior iliac spine, spread the middle finger towards the iliac crest; inject in the centre of the "V".
- **Vastus lateralis**: middle third of the outer thigh, between a hand's breadth below the greater trochanter and a hand's breadth above the knee.
- **Deltoid**: 2.5–5 cm (about 2–3 finger widths) below the acromion process, in the middle of the lateral arm.
- **Dorsogluteal**: upper outer quadrant of the buttock — taught for recognition, but many guidelines now advise using the ventrogluteal site instead.

**Contraindications for a site**: infection, bruising, scars, oedema, paralysis, lumps; for IM generally — bleeding disorders and anticoagulant therapy (needs care), poor muscle mass, shock (poor absorption).

**Aspiration**: aspiration before IM injection is no longer advised for vaccines, and practice for other drugs varies — follow your institution's policy.

**General steps for any injection**: check order and rights; hand hygiene; prepare at a clean surface; identify the patient; explain and give privacy; select and clean the site with alcohol swab and let it dry; insert with a quick dart-like motion at the right angle; inject slowly; withdraw at the same angle; press gently with dry cotton; discard the needle-syringe immediately into the sharps container without recapping; record the site, time and response.

**Z-track technique**: pull the skin and tissue laterally by about 2.5–3 cm before inserting; inject, wait about 10 seconds, withdraw, then release the skin — this seals the track and prevents leakage of irritant drugs into the tissue.

## 7.17 Equipment: syringes, needles, cannulas and infusion sets

- **Syringe parts**: tip (luer slip or luer lock), barrel with markings, flange, plunger with rubber bung. Sizes: 1 mL (tuberculin, insulin syringes marked in units), 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 50 mL.
- **Needle parts**: hub, shaft (cannula), bevel (slanted tip). **Gauge** = diameter — a higher number means a finer needle; length chosen by route and the patient's size.
- **IV cannula parts**: needle (stylet), catheter, hub, wings, injection port (in some types), cap.
- **Infusion set**: spike, drip chamber, roller clamp, tubing, injection port, luer connector. Macro-drip (adult) and micro-drip (60 drops/mL); blood sets have a filter; burette sets (measured chamber) for children.

## 7.18 Vials and ampoules

- **Ampoule**: sealed glass container with a neck; single use; contents liquid.
  Steps: tap the top to bring liquid down; protect the fingers with gauze or an ampoule opener and snap away from you; withdraw using a **filter needle** where available (prevents drawing glass particles); change to a fresh needle to inject; discard the glass in the sharps/glass container.
- **Vial**: glass or plastic bottle with a rubber stopper; single-dose or multi-dose; liquid or powder.
  Steps: remove the cap; clean the rubber top with alcohol; draw into the syringe air equal to the volume to be withdrawn and inject it into the vial — prevents a vacuum; invert and withdraw; remove air bubbles; for powders, add the stated diluent, roll gently to mix (do not shake vigorously); label a multi-dose vial with date, time, concentration and initials after opening and store as directed.
- **Mixing two drugs in one syringe** only when known to be compatible and as per policy.

## 7.19 Care of equipment, disposal and prevention of needle-stick injuries

**Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (colour coding, as amended)**

| Container | Waste |
| --- | --- |
| Yellow | Anatomical waste, items soiled with blood or body fluids, expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste |
| Red | Contaminated recyclable plastics — tubing, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, gloves |
| White (translucent, puncture-proof) | Sharps — needles, syringes with fixed needles, blades, scalpels |
| Blue (cardboard box with blue marking) | Glassware — broken glass, ampoules, vials (after decontamination as per rules) |

**Prevention of needle-stick injuries**
- **Never recap** used needles; if recapping is unavoidable, use the one-handed scoop method.
- Do not bend, break or remove needles by hand.
- Dispose immediately into a puncture-proof sharps container kept at the point of use; close it when three-quarters full.
- Use safety-engineered devices where available; get hepatitis B vaccination.
- Concentrate, keep good light, and get help with restless patients.

**If a needle-stick injury occurs**: let the wound bleed freely; wash with soap and running water (do not scrub, squeeze or apply bleach); splashes into eyes or mouth — rinse with plenty of water; report immediately to the in-charge; the source and exposed person are assessed; **post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)** is decided by the doctor and should be started as early as possible — ideally within 2 hours and not later than 72 hours; record and follow up.

## 7.20 Topical administration

**Application to skin and mucous membranes**: clean the area, wear gloves, apply a thin layer of cream or ointment with a spatula or gloved hand in the direction of hair growth; transdermal patch — remove the old one, apply to a clean, hairless site, rotate sites, date it.

**Direct application of liquids**: painting with swabs (for example antiseptic on the throat or a wound), **gargle** (the patient tilts the head back and gargles the prescribed solution, then spits out), **swabbing the throat** (use a tongue depressor and good light, swab the area with the prescribed solution without causing gagging).

**Insertion into body cavities**: rectal suppository (see Unit 4); **vaginal pessary or medicated packing** — lithotomy or dorsal recumbent position, insert with an applicator or gloved finger along the posterior wall about 5–7.5 cm, ask the patient to lie down for 10–15 minutes; give a perineal pad.

**Instillations (drops)**

| Site | Key steps |
| --- | --- |
| **Eye** | Head tilted back, look up; pull the lower lid down; drop into the **lower conjunctival sac**, not on the cornea; do not touch the eye with the dropper; ask the patient to close the eye gently; press the inner canthus for about 1 minute (reduces systemic absorption); separate dropper for each eye if infected; ointment applied from inner to outer canthus |
| **Ear** | Warm drops to room/body temperature (cold drops cause vertigo); patient lies with the affected ear up; **adult — pull the pinna up and back**; **child under 3 — down and back**; drop along the canal wall; stay on the side for 2–3 minutes |
| **Nose** | Blow the nose first; head tilted back (or position for the sinus to be reached); insert the dropper just inside the nostril without touching; stay in position for a few minutes |
| **Bladder** | Through a catheter with strict asepsis; retain for the ordered time |
| **Rectal** | Small-volume medicated enema or retention solution in left lateral position |

**Irrigations (washing out a cavity)**

| Site | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| Eye | Patient's head turned towards the affected side; flow from **inner to outer canthus** so fluid does not enter the other eye; for chemical splashes irrigate copiously |
| Ear | Warm solution; direct the stream along the roof of the canal, gently; not if the eardrum is perforated |
| Bladder | See Unit 4 |
| Vaginal (douche) | Only on order; lithotomy; low pressure, with the container held only a little above the hips |
| Rectal | Bowel wash (Unit 4) |

**Spraying**: nose (patient sitting, head slightly forward, nozzle into the nostril pointed away from the septum, spray while breathing in) and throat (with good light, tongue depressed, spray onto the back of the throat).

## 7.21 Inhalation

**Purposes**: deliver medicine directly to the airways, loosen secretions, moisten the airways, relieve congestion.

**Types**
- **Steam inhalation** — moist heat; simple bowl-and-towel method or a steam inhaler; keep the face about 20–30 cm away; never leave children unattended near hot water (scald risk).
- **Oxygen** (Unit 5).
- **Metered-dose inhaler (MDI)**: shake; breathe out fully; place the mouthpiece in the mouth (or use a **spacer**); press once as you begin a slow deep breath; hold the breath for about 10 seconds; wait before the next puff as instructed; **rinse the mouth after steroid inhalers** (prevents oral thrush).
- **Dry-powder inhaler**: load, breathe out away from the device, then breathe in quickly and deeply.
- **Nebuliser**: converts liquid medicine into a fine mist using compressed air or oxygen; patient sits upright and breathes normally through a mouthpiece or mask until the chamber is empty; clean and dry the parts after use.
- **Endotracheal or tracheal inhalation**: medicines or humidified air given through an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy, by in-line nebuliser or MDI adapter.

**Recording and reporting**: drug, method, time, the patient's breathing, pulse and SpO2 before and after, any side effects (tremor, rapid heart rate), and the effect on breathlessness.

## 7.22 Other parenteral routes (meaning only)

| Route | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Epidural | Into the epidural space outside the dura of the spinal cord (pain relief in labour or after surgery) |
| Intrathecal | Into the subarachnoid space (CSF) through a lumbar puncture |
| Intraosseous | Into the bone marrow cavity (usually the tibia) — emergency access in children and adults when veins cannot be found |
| Intraperitoneal | Into the peritoneal cavity (peritoneal dialysis, some chemotherapy) |
| Intrapleural | Into the pleural space |
| Intra-arterial | Into an artery (some chemotherapy, angiography) |
| Intracardiac | Into the heart (rarely used) |
| Intra-articular | Into a joint |

These are given by doctors or specially trained staff; the nurse prepares, assists, monitors and records.

## Remember

- ADME = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; first-pass effect for oral drugs.
- 10 rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, education, refusal, assessment, evaluation; check the label three times.
- Amount = (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity; same units first.
- 1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 µg; 1% = 1 g per 100 mL.
- Verbal orders: write, read back, get signed.
- ID 10–15°, SC 45°, IM 90°; ventrogluteal preferred, vastus lateralis for infants, avoid dorsogluteal.
- Never recap; sharps into white puncture-proof container; PEP ideally within 2 hours, not after 72 hours.
- Ear drops: adult pinna up and back; child under 3 down and back. Eye drops into the lower sac.
- Rinse the mouth after steroid inhalers; refrigerated drugs at 2–8 °C; controlled drugs double-locked with a register.
- Report and record every medication error; never hide it.
