# Unit 8: Sensory needs, care of the unconscious patient, and death and dying

INC Unit X (5 hours theory + 6 hours skill lab) — sensory experience, sensory alterations and their management, and care of the unconscious patient (with the Glasgow Coma Scale) — joined with INC Unit XI (4 hours theory + 6 hours skill lab) — loss, grief, theories of grief and dying, death, care of the dying, last office, mortuary procedures, and an overview of medico-legal cases, advance directives, DNR, organ donation and euthanasia.

## Part A: Sensory needs

## 8.1 Introduction and components of sensory experience

People need a steady, meaningful flow of sensory input to stay oriented and well. Illness, hospital environments and ageing can disturb it.

**Components of the sensory experience**

```text
Reception  →  Perception  →  Reaction
(stimulus     (brain gives    (the person
 reaches a     it meaning)     responds)
 receptor and
 nerve impulse
 travels)
```

- **Reception**: a stimulus (light, sound, touch, smell, taste, position) excites a sense receptor and is conducted to the brain.
- **Perception**: the brain integrates and interprets the stimulus, using memory and attention.
- **Reaction**: the person responds; the brain also filters out unimportant stimuli so that attention goes only to meaningful ones.

## 8.2 Arousal mechanism

The **reticular activating system (RAS)** in the brainstem receives sensory input and keeps the cerebral cortex awake and alert. Too little input lowers arousal; too much floods it. The RAS also controls the sleep–wake cycle — this is why noise and lights at night disturb patients.

## 8.3 Factors affecting sensory function

Age (presbyopia and hearing loss in the elderly; developing senses in infants), meaningful stimuli in the environment, amount of stimuli (ICU noise), social interaction, environment (isolation, darkness), culture, illness (diabetes affects vision and touch, stroke affects perception), medicines (some damage hearing; sedatives dull perception), and lifestyle (smoking dulls taste and smell, loud music damages hearing).

## 8.4 Assessment of sensory alterations

| Alteration | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sensory deficit** | Impaired reception or perception in one or more senses | Blindness, deafness, loss of touch after stroke, peripheral neuropathy |
| **Sensory deprivation** | Too little meaningful stimulation | Isolation rooms, bed rest, patching both eyes, elderly living alone |
| **Sensory overload** | Too many stimuli to process | ICU noise, alarms, constant procedures, pain |
| **Sensory poverty** | Long-term lack of varied, meaningful stimuli in daily life | Monotonous environment of long-stay institutions |

**Signs of deprivation**: boredom, restlessness, drowsiness, poor concentration, confusion, hallucinations, depression.
**Signs of overload**: anxiety, irritability, racing thoughts, poor sleep, disorientation, fatigue.

**Assessment**: history of sensory loss and aids used; mental status; vision, hearing, touch, taste, smell tests; the environment; ability to communicate; risk of injury.

## 8.5 Management of sensory alterations

- **Promote health**: screening (vision, hearing), protection from noise, eye protection at work, control of diabetes and blood pressure.
- **Prevent deprivation**: meaningful stimulation — conversation, radio, newspapers, clocks and calendars, family visits, pictures, touch, a window view; group activities.
- **Prevent overload**: reduce noise and light at night, cluster care to allow rest, explain procedures, limit visitors when needed, quiet room.
- **Safety**: orientation to the room, call bell within reach, night light, rails as needed, clear pathways, check bath water temperature for those with reduced touch.
- **Use and care of aids**: glasses, contact lenses, hearing aids (Unit 3).

### Promoting meaningful communication

| Patient | What helps |
| --- | --- |
| **Aphasia** (expressive — knows what to say but cannot say it; receptive — cannot understand speech; global — both) | Simple short sentences, one question at a time, yes/no questions, gestures, picture boards, give time, do not shout, do not finish sentences for them |
| **Artificial airway** (endotracheal tube, tracheostomy — cannot speak) | Writing board, letter or picture boards, call bell, yes/no questions with nods or blinks, lip-reading; speaking valves as ordered; explain that speech will return when the tube is out |
| **Visual impairment** | Announce yourself and say when you leave, speak in a normal tone, describe surroundings, use the clock method for meals, keep furniture in the same place, guide with the patient holding your elbow |
| **Hearing impairment** | Face the person in good light, get attention first, speak clearly and slightly slower (do not shout), reduce background noise, check the hearing aid, use writing or gestures, sign language interpreter if needed |

## Part B: Care of the unconscious patient

## 8.6 Definition, causes and risk factors

**Consciousness** is awareness of self and the environment with the ability to respond. **Unconsciousness** is an abnormal state in which the person is not aware of self or surroundings and cannot respond normally to stimuli; **coma** is the deepest state, from which the patient cannot be aroused even by painful stimuli.

**Causes (memory aid "AEIOU TIPS")**

| Letter | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| A | Alcohol, acidosis |
| E | Epilepsy (post-seizure), electrolyte imbalance, endocrine (thyroid, adrenal) |
| I | Insulin — hypoglycaemia or diabetic coma |
| O | Opioids and other overdose, oxygen lack (hypoxia) |
| U | Uraemia (kidney failure), liver failure |
| T | Trauma (head injury), temperature extremes |
| I | Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, sepsis) |
| P | Poisoning, psychiatric |
| S | Stroke, shock, space-occupying lesions (tumour, abscess) |

## 8.7 Pathophysiology

Consciousness needs the **RAS** in the brainstem and both cerebral hemispheres working. Unconsciousness results from (1) damage or pressure on the brainstem (bleeding, herniation from raised intracranial pressure), (2) widespread damage to both hemispheres, or (3) metabolic disturbances (low glucose, low oxygen, toxins) that depress neuronal function. Rising intracranial pressure reduces cerebral blood flow and can push brain tissue downward, compressing the brainstem.

## 8.8 Stages (levels) of consciousness

| Level | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Alert (conscious) | Awake, oriented, responds appropriately |
| Lethargy (drowsy) | Sleepy but wakes easily to voice; slow responses |
| Obtundation | Wakes with difficulty to loud voice or shaking; confused |
| Stupor (semi-coma) | Responds only to strong or painful stimuli; little speech |
| Coma | No response to any stimulus; deep coma — reflexes absent |

**Clinical manifestations**: reduced or absent response, abnormal breathing patterns (Cheyne–Stokes), changes in pupils (unequal, fixed, dilated in serious brain injury), abnormal posturing (decorticate — arms flexed; decerebrate — arms extended, worse sign), loss of protective reflexes (cough, gag, swallow, blink), incontinence, signs of raised intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, rising BP with slow pulse and irregular breathing — **Cushing's triad**).

## 8.9 Assessment: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

| Response | Score |
| --- | --- |
| **Eye opening (E)** | |
| Spontaneously | 4 |
| To speech (sound) | 3 |
| To pain (pressure) | 2 |
| None | 1 |
| **Verbal response (V)** | |
| Oriented | 5 |
| Confused | 4 |
| Inappropriate words | 3 |
| Incomprehensible sounds | 2 |
| None | 1 |
| **Motor response (M)** | |
| Obeys commands | 6 |
| Localises pain | 5 |
| Withdraws from pain (normal flexion) | 4 |
| Abnormal flexion (decorticate) | 3 |
| Extension (decerebrate) | 2 |
| None | 1 |

Total 3–15. **15** = fully conscious; **13–15** minor, **9–12** moderate, **8 or less** severe impairment (coma — the airway is at risk). Record each part separately (for example E2 V2 M4 = 8). A **fall of 2 or more points** is reported urgently. Also check pupils, limb movements and vital signs at each neurological check.

## 8.10 Nursing management of the unconscious patient

| Need | Nursing measures (with reasons) |
| --- | --- |
| **Airway** | Lateral or semi-prone position with the head slightly down/turned (tongue falls forward, secretions drain); oropharyngeal airway; suction as needed; never give anything by mouth |
| **Breathing** | Monitor rate, pattern and SpO2; oxygen as prescribed; chest physiotherapy; turn regularly |
| **Circulation** | Vital signs; fluid balance; prevent deep vein thrombosis — limb exercises, stockings as ordered |
| **Neurological** | GCS and pupils at ordered intervals; head end raised about 30° if raised intracranial pressure (and no contraindication); avoid neck flexion |
| **Nutrition and fluids** | IV fluids, NG feeds (check position each time), record intake–output and weight |
| **Elimination** | Indwelling catheter or condom drainage as ordered, catheter care; bowel care to prevent constipation |
| **Skin** | Turn 2-hourly, pressure-relieving mattress, keep dry, inspect pressure points (Braden score) |
| **Hygiene** | Daily bed bath, oral care every 2–4 hours (side-lying, swabs), hair and nail care |
| **Eyes** | Keep lids closed (tape or moist pads as ordered), artificial tears as prescribed — blink reflex is lost and the cornea dries and ulcerates |
| **Musculoskeletal** | Passive range-of-motion exercises, correct alignment, foot support to prevent foot drop, splints as advised |
| **Safety** | Side rails, padding, seizure precautions, temperature control |
| **Communication** | Talk to the patient and explain every action (hearing may remain), use the name, encourage family to talk and touch |
| **Family** | Information, emotional support, involve in care |

**Complications to prevent**: aspiration pneumonia, airway obstruction, pressure ulcers, contractures and foot drop, deep vein thrombosis, urinary infection, corneal ulcer, constipation, malnutrition, dehydration.

## Part C: Care of the terminally ill, death and dying

## 8.11 Loss, grief, bereavement and mourning

**Loss**: being without something one had and valued.

| Type of loss | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Actual | Death of a loved one, amputation |
| Perceived | Loss of self-confidence, status |
| Maturational (developmental) | Children leaving home, retirement, menopause |
| Situational | Job loss, divorce, disaster, illness |
| Anticipatory | Grieving before an expected loss (terminal diagnosis) |

- **Grief**: the emotional response to loss.
- **Bereavement**: the state of having lost someone to death.
- **Mourning**: the outward, culturally shaped expression of grief (rituals, customs, period of mourning).

**Types of grief responses**

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Normal (uncomplicated) | Common reactions that ease with time |
| Anticipatory | Grief before the actual loss |
| Complicated (dysfunctional) | Prolonged or intense grief that disrupts life — chronic, delayed, exaggerated or masked |
| Disenfranchised | Grief not openly accepted by society (miscarriage, death of a partner in a hidden relationship, pet) |

**Manifestations of grief**: crying, sadness, anger, guilt, anxiety, loneliness, disbelief; loss of appetite, sleep disturbance, fatigue, tightness in the chest; poor concentration, preoccupation with the deceased; social withdrawal.

**Factors influencing loss and grief responses**: age and development, relationship with the deceased, nature of the death (sudden, violent, suicide), personality and coping, social support, culture and religion, previous losses, socio-economic status.

## 8.12 Theories of grief and loss

**Kübler-Ross — five stages of dying**

| Stage | Typical words or behaviour | Nursing approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Denial | "Not me — the report must be wrong." | Accept without arguing or reinforcing; listen |
| Anger | "Why me?" — anger at staff, family, God | Do not take it personally; let feelings be expressed |
| Bargaining | "If I get better I will…" | Listen; support realistic hopes |
| Depression | Withdrawn, sad, crying | Be present, allow grief, touch, avoid false cheerfulness |
| Acceptance | Calm, making plans, saying goodbyes | Support wishes, involve family, ensure comfort |

The stages do not always follow this order; people move back and forth.

**Rando's "R" process model** — six processes of mourning:
1. **Recognise** the loss (acknowledge and understand the death).
2. **React** to the separation (feel and express the pain).
3. **Recollect** and re-experience the deceased and the relationship.
4. **Relinquish** old attachments to the deceased and the old assumptions about the world.
5. **Readjust** to move adaptively into the new world without forgetting the old.
6. **Reinvest** emotional energy in new relationships and goals.

## 8.13 Death

**Definition**: the permanent end of life.

- **Circulatory (cardiopulmonary) death**: irreversible stopping of heartbeat and breathing.
- **Brain death (brainstem death)**: irreversible loss of all brain function including the brainstem, while breathing and circulation may be kept going by machines. In India, brainstem death for organ donation is certified by a board of medical experts under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act and Rules, with tests repeated after a set interval (check the current Rules for the board's composition and the interval).

**Signs of impending death**: cold, mottled, bluish extremities; weak, rapid, irregular pulse and falling BP; noisy breathing from secretions ("death rattle"), Cheyne–Stokes breathing, periods of apnoea; decreased urine output; reduced consciousness; loss of swallowing; relaxed jaw; staring or glazed eyes; hearing often remains till late.

## 8.14 The dying patient's Bill of Rights (in summary)

The dying person has the right to: be treated as a living human being until death; keep hope; be cared for by those who maintain hope; express feelings and emotions about death in their own way; take part in decisions about care; expect continuing medical and nursing attention even when cure is no longer possible; not die alone; be free from pain; have honest answers to questions; not be deceived; receive help from and for the family in accepting death; die in peace and dignity; keep their individuality and not be judged for decisions; discuss and enlarge religious or spiritual experiences; expect that the body will be respected after death; and be cared for by caring, sensitive, knowledgeable people.

## 8.15 Care of the dying patient

- **Physical comfort**: pain relief as prescribed (regular, not only "when needed"), position change, mouth care (dry mouth), eye care, skin care, managing breathlessness (upright position, fan, oxygen if helpful), managing noisy secretions (positioning, gentle suction if needed), small sips and favourite foods, elimination care.
- **Psychological**: be present, listen, allow expression of fear and sadness, honest answers.
- **Spiritual**: arrange prayers, religious leader and rituals as wished.
- **Family**: open visiting, allow them to help in care, explain changes, prepare them for death, privacy.
- **Palliative care approach**: improves quality of life for patients and families facing life-limiting illness, through relief of pain and other physical, psychological, social and spiritual problems.

## 8.16 Physiological changes after death

| Change | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Algor mortis** | Gradual cooling of the body to room temperature |
| **Livor mortis** (post-mortem hypostasis) | Purple discolouration of dependent parts as blood settles by gravity; becomes fixed after some hours |
| **Rigor mortis** | Stiffening of muscles that begins a few hours after death in small muscles (eyelids, jaw), spreads to the whole body and later passes off; timing varies with temperature |
| Tissue softening, decomposition | Later changes by bacterial action, faster in heat |

Last office is therefore done soon after death, **before rigor mortis sets in**, so the body can be positioned naturally.

## 8.17 Death declaration, certification, autopsy and embalming

- **Declaration** of death is made by a doctor after examination (absence of pulse, heart sounds, breathing, fixed dilated pupils); the time is recorded.
- **Certification**: the doctor issues the medical certificate of cause of death (MCCD) under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969; the death must be registered with the local registrar (the hospital reports institutional deaths).
- **Autopsy (post-mortem examination)**: examination of the body after death to find the cause. **Medico-legal (police) autopsy** is compulsory in unnatural or suspicious deaths and is ordered by police or magistrate; **clinical (hospital) autopsy** needs the consent of the next of kin. For medico-legal cases, do not remove tubes, lines or dressings and preserve all evidence.
- **Embalming**: preserving the body with chemicals to delay decomposition, done by trained persons — for example when the body must be transported over a long distance or kept for a longer period.

## 8.18 Last office (death care)

**Purposes**: to keep the body clean and in a natural position; to prevent discharge and odour; to show respect; to identify the body correctly; to support the relatives.

**Main steps**
1. Confirm that death has been declared and recorded; inform the nurse in charge; check for any religious or cultural wishes and whether it is a medico-legal case or organ/eye donation (eye donation must happen within a few hours).
2. Allow the family time with the body in privacy.
3. Wear gloves and apron (standard precautions).
4. Lay the body flat, one pillow under the head (prevents blood pooling and discolouring the face); close the eyes gently with moist cotton; close the mouth (support the jaw with a rolled towel or bandage); replace dentures if possible.
5. Remove tubes, catheters and lines (unless medico-legal); cover wounds with clean dressings; pack orifices only where policy requires.
6. Bathe as needed, comb hair, put on a clean gown or as the family wishes.
7. List valuables and belongings with a witness and hand them over to the relatives against signature; leave the wedding ring or religious articles if the family wishes, taped and recorded.
8. Attach **identification labels** (name, age, sex, hospital number, ward, date and time of death) — usually to the wrist or ankle and on the outer wrap.
9. Wrap in a clean sheet (and a body bag if infectious), straighten the limbs, hands by the side.
10. Shift to the mortuary as per policy; clean and disinfect the unit; complete the records.

## 8.19 Counselling and supporting grieving relatives

Inform with sensitivity in a private room; use simple, clear words ("He has died"); allow expression of grief; stay with them; answer questions honestly; help with practical matters (formalities, belongings, transport); respect cultural and religious practices; give information about support services; recognise signs of complicated grief and refer.

## 8.20 Mortuary: placing and releasing the body

- **Placing**: the body is shifted on a covered trolley through a route that avoids public areas; identity checked and entered in the mortuary register with time; kept in a cold chamber.
- **Releasing**: verify the identity of the body and the person receiving it (relationship, ID proof); check that the death certificate is issued and, in medico-legal cases, police clearance and post-mortem are complete; hand over belongings; record the time and signatures of the receiving person and the staff.

## 8.21 Overview: medico-legal and ethical issues at the end of life

- **Medico-legal cases (MLC)**: injuries from road accidents, assault, burns, poisoning, suicide attempts, unnatural or suspicious deaths. Inform the police through the hospital's MLC procedure, record accurately, preserve evidence (clothes, bullets, poison samples, gastric contents), keep records safely.
- **Advance directive (living will)**: a written statement made by a competent adult about the treatment they want or refuse if they later lose the capacity to decide. In India the Supreme Court recognised living wills and passive euthanasia in *Common Cause v. Union of India* (2018) with procedural safeguards (later simplified by the court in 2023).
- **DNR / DNI (do not resuscitate / do not intubate)**: a written medical order, after discussion with the patient or family, that CPR or intubation will not be done if the heart or breathing stops. All other care continues.
- **Organ donation**: governed by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act; donors may be living (close relatives, with authorisation committees in other cases) or deceased (after brainstem death, with consent of the family). Eye (cornea) donation is possible after circulatory death within a few hours. NOTTO is the national body co-ordinating organ donation. The nurse identifies potential donors, informs the transplant co-ordinator, and supports the family.
- **Euthanasia**: deliberately ending life to relieve suffering. **Active euthanasia** (giving a substance to cause death) is illegal in India. **Passive euthanasia** (withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment) is permitted only under the procedure laid down by the Supreme Court (Aruna Shanbaug case, 2011, and Common Cause, 2018).

## Remember

- Sensory experience: reception → perception → reaction; the RAS keeps us alert.
- Deficit (organ problem), deprivation (too little), overload (too much), poverty (long-term lack of variety).
- Aphasia: short simple sentences, yes/no questions, picture boards, give time.
- GCS: E4 V5 M6 = 15; 8 or less = coma; a fall of 2 points is urgent.
- Unconscious patient: lateral position, nothing by mouth, eyes closed and moist, turn 2-hourly, talk to the patient.
- Kübler-Ross: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance.
- Rando: recognise, react, recollect, relinquish, readjust, reinvest.
- Algor (cooling), livor (pooling), rigor (stiffening) — do last office before rigor sets in.
- MLC: do not remove tubes or dressings; preserve evidence.
- Active euthanasia is illegal in India; passive euthanasia and living wills only under Supreme Court guidelines.

# Unit 9: Psychosocial needs — self-concept, sexuality, stress and adaptation, culture and spirituality

INC Units XII–XV, grouped in the syllabus as "Psychosocial needs (A–D)": A. Self-concept (3 hours), B. Sexuality (2 hours), C. Stress and adaptation (2 hours theory + 4 hours skill lab), D. Cultural diversity and spirituality (6 hours). Holistic care means meeting these needs as well as physical ones.

## Part A: Self-concept

## 9.1 Introduction

**Self-concept** is the mental picture a person has of himself or herself — the beliefs and feelings about who one is. It develops from birth through interaction with family, friends, school and society, and it changes with life events, illness and ageing. A healthy self-concept helps a person cope with illness; a damaged one can lead to anxiety, depression and poor co-operation with treatment.

## 9.2 Components of self-concept

| Component | Meaning | Threats in illness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Personal identity** | The sense of being a unique individual — name, gender, roles, values, beliefs | Confusion, dementia, loss of independence |
| **Body image** | The mental picture of one's body — appearance, size, function | Amputation, mastectomy, colostomy, burns scars, hair loss, obesity, paralysis |
| **Role performance** | How a person carries out expected roles (parent, worker, student) | Hospital stay, disability, job loss, retirement |
| **Self-esteem** | The value a person places on himself or herself — feelings of self-worth | Failure, criticism, chronic illness, dependence, stigma |

**Role terms**: role conflict (two roles with incompatible demands — a nurse-mother with a sick child at home), role ambiguity (unclear expectations), role strain (feeling unable to fulfil a role), role overload (too many roles).

## 9.3 Factors affecting self-concept

Developmental stage, family relationships and early experiences, culture, illness and disability, surgery affecting appearance or function, trauma, abuse, success and failure, relationships, ageing, media images, and stressors.

## 9.4 Nursing management

1. **Assessment**: ask how the patient feels about self and the illness ("How do you feel about the change in your body?"), observe behaviour — avoiding looking at a wound, negative self-talk, withdrawal, excessive dependence, poor grooming.
2. **Nursing diagnoses**: disturbed body image; situational low self-esteem; ineffective role performance; disturbed personal identity.
3. **Interventions**:
   - Accept the patient warmly; show respect; call by name.
   - Encourage expression of feelings; listen without judging.
   - Help the patient look at and touch the changed body part gradually, when ready.
   - Teach self-care skills (stoma care, use of prosthesis) — independence builds self-esteem.
   - Point out strengths and give honest praise for achievements.
   - Involve family; prepare them for the patient's changed appearance.
   - Arrange contact with support groups and people who have adapted to similar changes.
   - Respect privacy and modesty during care.
4. **Evaluation**: patient talks about the change, takes part in care, resumes roles, expresses positive statements about self.

## Part B: Sexuality

## 9.5 Sexual development throughout life

**Sexuality** includes a person's sexual feelings, identity, attitudes, relationships and behaviour, and is part of total well-being.

| Stage | Development |
| --- | --- |
| Infancy and early childhood | Develops gender identity (awareness of being a boy or girl) by about 2–3 years; curiosity about body parts |
| School age | Learns gender roles; same-sex friendships; questions about reproduction |
| Adolescence | Puberty — secondary sexual characteristics, menarche, nocturnal emissions; strong sexual feelings; sexual identity and orientation become clearer; risk of unsafe sexual behaviour |
| Young adulthood | Intimate relationships, marriage or partnership, family planning |
| Middle age | Menopause in women; slower sexual response in men; changes in body image |
| Older adulthood | Sexual interest often continues; physical changes (vaginal dryness, slower erection) and illness or medicines may affect function; need for intimacy and touch remains |

## 9.6 Sexual health and sexual orientation

- **Sexual health** (WHO): a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality — not only the absence of disease; it needs a positive, respectful approach and the possibility of pleasurable and safe sexual experiences free of coercion, discrimination and violence.
- **Sexual orientation**: the pattern of emotional and sexual attraction — heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual and others. **Gender identity** is the inner sense of being male, female, both or neither, which may differ from the sex assigned at birth (transgender persons). In India the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 protects against discrimination, and consensual same-sex relations between adults are not a crime since the Supreme Court judgment of 2018 (Navtej Singh Johar). The nurse gives non-judgemental care to every person.

## 9.7 Factors affecting sexuality

Physical illness (diabetes, heart disease, spinal injury), surgery (mastectomy, hysterectomy, prostate surgery, stoma), medicines (some antihypertensives and antidepressants), pregnancy and post-partum period, ageing, psychological factors (stress, depression, anxiety, body image, past abuse), relationship problems, culture and religion, alcohol and drug use, and lack of knowledge.

## 9.8 Prevention of STIs, unwanted pregnancy, sexual harassment and abuse

**Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**: health education about abstinence, mutual faithfulness, correct and consistent condom use, avoiding multiple partners; early treatment of STIs for both partners; screening in pregnancy; hepatitis B and HPV vaccination as per national schedules; reducing stigma so that people seek care.

**Unwanted pregnancy**: information on family planning methods (temporary — condoms, oral pills, IUCD, injectables; permanent — tubectomy, vasectomy) and emergency contraception as available under the national family planning programme; counselling of adolescents and couples; safe abortion services within the law (the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, as amended).

**Sexual harassment and abuse**
- Teach children about "safe and unsafe touch" and to tell a trusted adult.
- In India, sexual offences against children are dealt with under the **POCSO Act, 2012**, which makes reporting compulsory; workplace sexual harassment is covered by the **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013** (internal complaints committees).
- Nurses: recognise signs of abuse (injuries in different stages of healing, fear, withdrawal, STIs in children), give care with privacy and a female attendant, document accurately, preserve evidence and follow the hospital's medico-legal procedure.

## 9.9 Dealing with inappropriate sexual behaviour

Patients may make sexual remarks, touch staff inappropriately or expose themselves (sometimes because of confusion, dementia, brain injury or medicines).

1. Stay calm and professional; do not laugh it off or encourage it.
2. Set clear limits firmly: "Please do not touch me. That is not acceptable."
3. Redirect the patient to the task; leave if the behaviour continues and get help.
4. Assess for causes (confusion, medicines, unmet need for intimacy).
5. Report to the nurse in charge and record the facts; plan consistent responses in the team (care in pairs if needed).
6. Nurses have the right to work without harassment; use the institution's complaint mechanism.

## Part C: Stress and adaptation

## 9.10 Introduction and types of stress

- **Stress**: a state produced by a change in the environment that is perceived as challenging, threatening or damaging to the person's balance.
- **Stressor**: any event or stimulus that causes stress.
- **Adaptation**: the process of adjusting to stressors to keep balance (**homeostasis**).

**Types of stress**: **eustress** (positive, motivating — exam preparation, a new job) and **distress** (negative, harmful); **acute** (short-term) and **chronic** (long-lasting, as in caring for a chronically ill family member).

**Sources of stress**: internal (illness, fear, low self-esteem) and external (work, family, finances, environment); developmental (normal life changes — adolescence, retirement) and situational (accident, hospitalisation, divorce).

**Types of stressors**: **physical** (heat, cold, noise, trauma), **physiological** (pain, infection, hunger, fatigue), **psychological** (fear, loss, conflict), **social and cultural** (poverty, unemployment, discrimination), **chemical** (drugs, pollutants), **microbiological**.

**Effects and indicators of stress**: in mild amounts stress improves alertness and performance; excessive or prolonged stress lowers immunity, raises BP, and contributes to headache, peptic ulcer, heart disease, sleep problems, anxiety and depression.

## 9.11 Stress adaptation: General and Local Adaptation Syndromes (Hans Selye)

**General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)** — the whole-body response:

```text
1. ALARM REACTION        Stressor recognised; "fight or flight":
   (shock → countershock) sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla
                          release adrenaline; cortisol rises;
                          heart rate, BP, breathing, blood sugar rise;
                          pupils dilate
            ↓
2. RESISTANCE (adaptation) Body tries to adapt; hormone levels
                          stay raised but stabilise; if the stressor
                          is removed, the body returns to normal
            ↓
3. EXHAUSTION             Adaptive energy runs out if the stressor
                          continues; resistance falls; illness or
                          even death may follow
```

**Local Adaptation Syndrome (LAS)** — a localised response of a tissue, organ or body part; short-term and aimed at restoring balance. Examples:
- **Reflex pain response**: withdrawing a hand from a hot object.
- **Inflammatory response**: redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function around an injury to limit damage and promote healing.

If the local response is not enough, the GAS is activated.

## 9.12 Manifestations of stress

| Physical | Psychological / behavioural |
| --- | --- |
| Rapid pulse, raised BP, rapid breathing | Anxiety, fear, irritability, anger |
| Dilated pupils, sweating, cold clammy hands | Poor concentration, forgetfulness |
| Dry mouth, nausea, loss of appetite or overeating | Crying, withdrawal, restlessness |
| Headache, muscle tension, back pain | Sleep disturbance |
| Raised blood sugar | Use of alcohol, tobacco or drugs |
| Fatigue, lowered immunity | Loss of interest, depression |

## 9.13 Coping strategies and mechanisms

**Coping** is the way a person deals with stress.

- **Problem-focused coping**: acting on the problem (seeking information, planning, making changes).
- **Emotion-focused coping**: managing the feelings (talking to a friend, prayer, relaxation, crying).
- **Adaptive** coping reduces stress and helps (exercise, support, problem solving); **maladaptive** coping gives short relief but causes harm (alcohol, avoidance, aggression).

**Ego defence mechanisms** (unconscious ways of reducing anxiety) — useful in small amounts, harmful if overused:

| Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Denial | Refusing to believe a diagnosis |
| Projection | Blaming others for one's own feelings |
| Rationalisation | Giving acceptable reasons for failure |
| Displacement | Shouting at the nurse when angry with the doctor |
| Regression | Returning to childlike behaviour when ill |
| Repression | Pushing painful memories out of awareness |
| Sublimation | Channelling feelings into acceptable activity (sport, art) |
| Compensation | Excelling in one area to make up for weakness in another |

## 9.14 Stress management

**Assisting with coping and adaptation**
1. Assess stressors, stress level, coping methods and support.
2. Give information about the illness and procedures — reduces fear of the unknown.
3. Encourage expression of feelings; listen actively.
4. Teach relaxation techniques: deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, meditation, yoga as appropriate.
5. Encourage problem solving, time management, adequate sleep, a balanced diet, regular exercise, and avoidance of alcohol and tobacco.
6. Mobilise family and social support; refer to counselling or support groups when needed; crisis intervention when coping fails.

**Creating a therapeutic environment**
- Physical: clean, quiet, well-lit, ventilated, safe, with privacy and some personal belongings; reduce noise at night.
- Psychological and social: warm, accepting attitude; respect and dignity; consistent staff; clear routines; family involvement; opportunity to make choices.

**Recreational and diversion therapies**: reading, music, television or radio, games (carrom, chess, cards), art and craft, gardening, group activities, outings for long-stay patients, play therapy for children, occupational therapy. They reduce boredom, anxiety and pain perception and improve mood and social interaction.

## Part D: Cultural diversity and spirituality

## 9.15 Cultural concepts

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Culture** | The shared, learned values, beliefs, customs and ways of life of a group, passed from generation to generation |
| **Subculture** | A smaller group within a larger culture with its own distinctive patterns (tribal communities, a religious sect, adolescents) |
| **Multicultural** | A society or setting in which many cultures live together |
| **Diversity** | Differences among people — ethnicity, religion, language, gender, age, ability, economic status |
| **Race** | A grouping of people by shared physical (biological) characteristics such as skin colour |
| **Ethnicity** | Belonging to a group with a shared cultural heritage, language and origin |
| **Acculturation** | Adopting some practices of another (dominant) culture while keeping one's own |
| **Assimilation** | Gradually taking on the dominant culture's patterns so fully that the original culture is largely lost |
| **Ethnocentrism** | Believing one's own culture is superior and judging others by it — a barrier to care |
| **Stereotyping** | Assuming all members of a group are the same |

## 9.16 Transcultural nursing and cultural competence

**Transcultural nursing** (founded by **Madeleine Leininger**, theory of culture care diversity and universality, illustrated by the **Sunrise model**) is the study and practice of nursing that compares cultures' health beliefs and practices, and gives care that fits the person's culture. Leininger's three modes of action: **culture care preservation/maintenance**, **culture care accommodation/negotiation**, and **culture care repatterning/restructuring**.

**Cultural competence** is the ability to give effective care to people of different cultures. Campinha-Bacote describes five constructs:
1. **Cultural awareness** — examining one's own biases.
2. **Cultural knowledge** — learning about other cultures' beliefs and health practices.
3. **Cultural skill** — collecting cultural data in assessment.
4. **Cultural encounters** — interacting directly with people of different cultures.
5. **Cultural desire** — genuine motivation to become culturally competent.

## 9.17 Providing culturally responsive care

- Assess cultural beliefs: language, religion, diet (vegetarian, halal, fasting), modesty and touch, family decision-making, beliefs about illness causes, use of traditional medicine (AYUSH remedies, home remedies), birth and death customs.
- Use a trained interpreter, not children of the family, for important information.
- Respect modesty — same-sex caregiver where requested; expose only what is needed.
- Allow religious articles (threads, amulets) unless they interfere with treatment; discuss when removal is necessary.
- Adjust diet and timing of medicines during fasting where safe, after consulting the doctor.
- Include the family as the patient wishes; explain in simple words; check understanding.
- Avoid stereotyping — ask each person what matters to them.

## 9.18 Spirituality

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Spirituality** | A person's search for meaning and purpose in life and connection with self, others, nature and a higher power; broader than religion |
| **Faith** | Belief in or commitment to something or someone (often a higher power) that cannot be proven |
| **Hope** | Expectation of a good future; gives energy to cope |
| **Religion** | An organised system of beliefs, practices, rituals and worship shared by a community |
| **Spiritual well-being** | A sense of harmony, meaning and peace — vertical (relationship with God or a higher power) and horizontal (relationships with self, others and the world) |

**Factors affecting spirituality**: age and development, family and culture, life experiences, illness and suffering, hospitalisation (separation from usual practices and community), crisis and loss, the nurse's own attitudes.

**Spiritual problems in illness**
- **Acute illness**: sudden illness may make a person question beliefs ("Why has God done this to me?") or turn to prayer for strength.
- **Chronic illness**: long dependence and suffering can lead to hopelessness, anger with God, or growth in faith.
- **Terminal illness**: fear of death, regrets, need for forgiveness and reconciliation, search for meaning.
- **Near-death experience**: people who survive a close brush with death may describe seeing a light, leaving the body or peace; they need to be listened to without judgement and may change their values afterwards.

**Spiritual distress**: disturbance in the person's belief or value system that gives strength, hope and meaning. Signs: questioning the meaning of life or suffering, anger at God, feeling abandoned, guilt, inability to pray or join religious practices, hopelessness, sleep disturbance.

## 9.19 Dealing with spiritual distress

1. Assess spiritual needs (beliefs, practices, sources of strength — for example the FICA questions: Faith, Importance, Community, Address in care).
2. Be present; listen with empathy; accept the person's beliefs even if different from your own; do not impose your beliefs.
3. Support religious practices — prayer time, scriptures, prayer beads, a quiet place, dietary rules, rituals before surgery or death.
4. Arrange visits by a priest, pandit, maulvi, granthi or other spiritual leader as the patient wishes.
5. Encourage hope (realistic goals, meaningful activities, life review, contact with loved ones).
6. Help the patient find meaning — talk about life events and achievements, forgiveness and reconciliation.
7. Respect cultural and religious customs around death and the care of the body.

## Remember

- Self-concept components: personal identity, body image, role performance, self-esteem.
- Body-image threats: amputation, mastectomy, stoma, burns, alopecia — encourage gradual looking and self-care.
- Sexual health is well-being, not only absence of disease; give non-judgemental care to all orientations and gender identities.
- POCSO Act 2012 — mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse.
- Inappropriate sexual behaviour: calm, firm limits, redirect, report, record.
- Selye's GAS: alarm → resistance → exhaustion; LAS: reflex pain and inflammatory responses.
- Eustress positive; distress harmful; coping problem-focused or emotion-focused.
- Acculturation keeps the old culture; assimilation largely replaces it.
- Leininger = transcultural nursing (Sunrise model); Campinha-Bacote = awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire.
- Spirituality is broader than religion; support practices, listen, involve spiritual leaders as wished.

# Unit 10: First aid and emergencies

This unit is **Unit XIV of Nursing Foundation I** (First Aid, 20 hours theory + 20 hours skill lab, taught with the mandatory First Aid module of NDMA / Indian Red Cross Society). It is included here because the university paper "Nursing Foundations II including First Aid" examines Nursing Foundation I and II together. Steps follow standard first-aid principles as taught by the Indian Red Cross Society and international first-aid guidelines; local protocols may differ slightly — follow your institution's current version. First aid here never involves giving medicines; the first aider's job is to keep the person safe until medical help takes over.

## 10.1 Definition, aims, principles, scope and rules

**First aid** is the immediate help given to a sick or injured person, with materials at hand, until professional medical help arrives.

**Aims (the 3 Ps)**
1. **Preserve life**.
2. **Prevent** the condition from getting worse.
3. **Promote** recovery.

**Basic principles**
1. Ensure **safety** — of yourself, bystanders and the casualty (danger first).
2. Assess quickly and systematically; treat life-threatening problems first (**primary survey**).
3. Call for help early — national emergency **112**, ambulance **108** (in most states).
4. Do no further harm; work within your training.
5. Reassure the casualty; keep them warm and comfortable.
6. Arrange transport to hospital; hand over clearly.

**Scope**: injuries at home, road, school, workplace; sudden illness (fainting, seizures, heart attack, stroke, asthma); poisoning, bites, burns; disasters and community emergencies.

**Rules (golden rules)**
- Do first things first, quickly but calmly.
- Get consent if the person is conscious; act in their interest if unconscious.
- Use standard precautions (gloves or a barrier) for blood and body fluids.
- Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person, a person likely to need surgery, or a person who cannot swallow.
- Do not move a casualty unnecessarily, especially if spinal injury is possible.
- Do not remove embedded objects.
- Record what happened and what you did; hand over to the professional.

## 10.2 Primary survey: DR CAB

```text
D — Danger      Is the scene safe? Remove the danger or the casualty.
R — Response    Tap the shoulders and shout "Are you all right?"
                No response → shout for help; call 112/108; ask for an AED.
C — Circulation If not breathing normally → start chest compressions.
A — Airway      Head-tilt chin-lift (jaw thrust if spinal injury suspected).
B — Breathing   Look, listen and feel for no more than 10 seconds.
                Gasping is NOT normal breathing.
```

If the casualty is breathing normally but unconscious, place in the **recovery position** and keep checking breathing. Then do a **secondary survey** (head-to-toe check, history — what happened, symptoms, allergies, medicines, past illness, last meal).

## 10.3 Respiratory emergencies and basic CPR

### Adult basic life support (cardiopulmonary resuscitation)
1. Scene safe → unresponsive → call for help, call 112/108, send for an AED.
2. Open the airway and check for normal breathing (no more than 10 seconds).
3. Not breathing normally → **chest compressions**: heel of one hand on the **centre of the chest (lower half of the sternum)**, other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over hands.
4. Compress **5–6 cm** deep, at **100–120 per minute**; allow the chest to recoil fully; minimise interruptions.
5. If trained and willing, give **30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths** (each breath over about 1 second, enough to make the chest rise). If not trained or unwilling, give **continuous chest compressions (hands-only CPR)**.
6. **AED**: switch on and follow the voice prompts; pads on bare chest (below the right collarbone and on the left side below the armpit); no one touches the casualty during analysis and shock; resume CPR at once after the shock.
7. Continue until the person breathes normally, help takes over, you are exhausted, or the scene becomes unsafe.

**Children and infants (trained rescuer)**: start with 5 rescue breaths if trained; compress at least one-third of the chest depth (about 4 cm in infants with two fingers or two thumbs; about 5 cm in children with one or two hands); ratio 30:2 (or 15:2 for trained health workers working in pairs, as per protocol).

### Choking (foreign body in the airway)

| Situation | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Mild (can cough, speak, breathe) | Encourage coughing; do not slap the back; stay with them |
| Severe adult or child over 1 year (cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively) | Up to **5 back blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand while the person leans forward; then up to **5 abdominal thrusts** (Heimlich manoeuvre) — fist above the navel below the breastbone, pull sharply inward and upward; alternate 5 and 5 |
| Pregnant or very obese | Use **chest thrusts** instead of abdominal thrusts |
| Infant under 1 year | Face-down along your forearm, head lower than body: **5 back blows**, then turn face-up: **5 chest thrusts** with two fingers; no abdominal thrusts |
| Becomes unconscious | Lower to the ground, call for help, start CPR; look in the mouth before breaths and remove a visible object; no blind finger sweeps |

### Other respiratory emergencies
- **Asthma attack**: sit upright leaning slightly forward, keep calm, help the person use their own reliever inhaler (as prescribed for them), loosen tight clothing, call for help if no improvement.
- **Drowning**: get the person out safely (reach or throw, do not go in unless trained); start with rescue breaths if trained, then CPR; keep warm.
- **Suffocation and strangulation**: remove the cause, open the airway, CPR if needed.
- **Smoke inhalation**: move to fresh air, check breathing, get help.

## 10.4 Wounds and haemorrhage

**Types of wounds**: abrasion (graze), incised (clean cut), laceration (torn, irregular), puncture (narrow, deep — nail, knife), avulsion (tissue torn away), amputation, crush, gunshot.

**Bleeding**: arterial (bright red, spurting), venous (dark red, steady flow), capillary (oozing). External or internal (suspect internal bleeding after blunt injury with signs of shock).

**First aid for external bleeding**
1. Wear gloves or use a barrier.
2. Apply **firm, direct pressure** over the wound with a clean pad or cloth (or with the hand if nothing else).
3. Keep pressing — if blood soaks through, place another pad on top and press harder; do not remove the first pad.
4. Apply a bandage firm enough to keep pressure, but check circulation beyond it.
5. For life-threatening bleeding from a limb not controlled by direct pressure, a **tourniquet** (commercial or improvised wide band) is applied above the wound by those trained; note the time.
6. Lay the casualty down, treat for shock, call 112/108.

**Special points**: **embedded object** — do not remove; press around it and pad on both sides. **Nosebleed** — sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes, breathe through the mouth; do not tilt the head back. **Amputated part** — wrap in a clean moist cloth, put in a plastic bag, keep the bag on ice (do not put the part directly on ice), send with the casualty.

**Minor wounds**: wash with clean running water, cover with a clean dressing, advise tetanus protection.

## 10.5 Shock

**Shock** is a life-threatening failure of circulation in which tissues do not get enough oxygen. Causes: severe bleeding, fluid loss (burns, diarrhoea), heart failure, severe infection, severe allergy (anaphylaxis), spinal injury.

**Signs**: pale, cold, clammy skin; rapid weak pulse; rapid shallow breathing; thirst; anxiety, restlessness, then drowsiness; low blood pressure; reduced urine.

**First aid**
1. Treat the cause (control bleeding).
2. Lay the casualty flat; raise the legs if there is no injury to the legs, hips or spine (helps blood return to the vital organs).
3. Loosen tight clothing; keep warm with a blanket (do not overheat).
4. Nothing by mouth; reassure.
5. Monitor breathing and response; call 112/108; be ready to start CPR.

**Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)**: swelling of face and throat, wheeze, rash, collapse — call for help immediately, help the person use their own prescribed adrenaline auto-injector if they carry one, keep them sitting (breathing difficulty) or lying with legs raised (faint), and be ready for CPR.

## 10.6 Musculoskeletal injuries

**Fracture** — a break in a bone. Types: closed (simple), open (compound — bone breaks the skin), complicated (with damage to nerves, vessels or organs); greenstick (children), comminuted, impacted.

**Signs**: pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, abnormal movement, crepitus, loss of function, shortening.

**First aid for fractures**
1. Keep the casualty still; support the injured part in the position found.
2. Control bleeding of an open fracture with pressure **around** the wound and cover it with a sterile dressing; do not push bone ends back.
3. **Immobilise** — the joint above and the joint below — using splints (padded boards, rolled newspaper), slings or by bandaging to the body (arm to chest, leg to the other leg), with padding in hollows.
4. Check circulation beyond the bandage (colour, warmth, pulse).
5. Treat for shock; arrange transport.
6. Do not try to straighten the limb unless trained and circulation is lost.

**Dislocation**: a bone displaced from its joint — severe pain, deformity, loss of movement. Support in a comfortable position, do not try to put it back, apply a cold pack, immobilise and get medical help.

**Muscle injuries (sprains, strains)**: **RICE** — **R**est, **I**ce or cold pack wrapped in cloth (about 20 minutes at a time), **C**ompression with a crepe bandage, **E**levation; seek medical advice if severe.

**Head and spinal injuries**: suspect spinal injury after falls from a height, diving, road accidents. Keep the head and neck still in line with the body (manual in-line support), do not move unless in danger, call for help, monitor breathing. If the airway is at risk, use the jaw thrust and, if the casualty must be turned, a **log roll** with several helpers.

## 10.7 Transportation of injured persons

**Principles**: transport only after life-threatening conditions are dealt with and injuries are immobilised; choose the method by the injury, the distance and the number of helpers; keep the casualty under observation; move smoothly; protect yourself (bend knees, keep the back straight, lift with the legs).

| Method | When used |
| --- | --- |
| Human crutch | Casualty can walk with support (minor leg injury) |
| Cradle carry | Children and light adults |
| Pick-a-back | Conscious light casualty who can hold on |
| Fireman's lift | Unconscious light casualty, single rescuer (not with spinal injuries) |
| Drag (blanket or shoulder drag) | Removing quickly from danger (fire, traffic) |
| Two-handed and four-handed seat | Conscious casualty, two rescuers |
| Fore-and-aft carry | Two rescuers, casualty unable to help |
| Chair carry | Through narrow passages or stairs |
| Stretcher (improvised with blanket and poles) | Serious injuries, longer distances; spinal board for spinal injury |

Carry a stretcher feet first normally; head first up stairs and hills (keeps the head higher).

## 10.8 Unconsciousness

1. DR CAB; if breathing normally, put in the **recovery position**:

```text
Kneel beside the casualty → near arm at a right angle →
far hand against the near cheek → bend the far knee →
pull on the knee to roll the casualty towards you →
tilt the head back to keep the airway open → upper leg at right angles
```

2. Check for injuries, medical bracelets; loosen tight clothing; keep warm.
3. Nothing by mouth; monitor breathing until help arrives.

**Fainting (syncope)**: lay the person down and raise the legs; loosen clothing; fresh air; recovers in a minute or so — if not, treat as unconscious.

**Seizures (fits)**: protect from injury (move hard objects away, cushion the head); do not restrain; **put nothing in the mouth**; note the time; after the jerking stops, place in the recovery position; call for help if the fit lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or it is the first fit, or the person is injured or pregnant.

**Low blood sugar in a known diabetic who is conscious and can swallow**: give sugar, a sweet drink or glucose; if unconscious, nothing by mouth — recovery position and call for help.

**Stroke**: recognise with **FAST** — **F**ace drooping, **A**rm weakness, **S**peech difficulty, **T**ime to call for help. Note the time symptoms started.

**Heart attack**: chest pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, sweating, breathlessness — sit comfortably (half-sitting), keep calm, call for help immediately, be ready for CPR.

## 10.9 Foreign bodies

| Site | First aid |
| --- | --- |
| **Skin** (splinter, thorn) | Remove a small superficial splinter with clean tweezers in line with entry, clean and cover; leave deep or large objects in place and pad around them |
| **Eye** | Do not rub; for loose particles, blink, wash with clean water from the inner corner outward, or lift with a moist cloth corner from the white of the eye; for embedded objects or chemicals — do not remove the object; cover the eye lightly (both eyes if possible to limit movement) and get help; chemicals — irrigate with plenty of clean water for a long time |
| **Ear** | Do not probe; tilt the head to let the object fall out; a live insect may come out if the ear is turned towards a light or with gentle flooding of lukewarm water only if the eardrum is known to be intact — otherwise seek help |
| **Nose** | Breathe through the mouth; close the unaffected nostril and blow gently; do not probe; seek help |
| **Throat** | See choking (10.3); for a fish bone, do not try to push it down — seek medical help |
| **Stomach (swallowed objects)** | Most small smooth objects pass; do not induce vomiting; seek medical advice — urgent for button batteries, magnets, sharp objects, or if pain, vomiting or drooling occurs |

## 10.10 Burns and scalds

**Burns** are caused by dry heat, flames, chemicals, electricity, radiation or friction; **scalds** by hot liquids or steam.

**Depth**: superficial (epidermis — red, painful, no blisters), partial thickness (blisters, very painful), full thickness (white, brown or charred, leathery, may be painless).

**Extent — Rule of Nines (adult)**: head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, front of trunk 18%, back of trunk 18%, each lower limb 18%, perineum 1%. The casualty's palm with fingers is about 1% of body surface (useful for small, scattered burns). Children have proportionally larger heads, so a different chart is used.

**First aid for heat burns and scalds**
1. **Stop the burning**: "Stop, drop and roll" for clothes on fire; smother with a blanket; remove from the source.
2. **Cool the burn with cool running water for at least 20 minutes** as soon as possible — reduces pain, depth and swelling. Keep the rest of the body warm (risk of hypothermia, especially in children).
3. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts — but not clothing stuck to the burn.
4. **Cover** loosely with cling film (laid lengthwise, not wrapped tightly round a limb) or a clean, non-fluffy cloth.
5. Do **not** apply ice, toothpaste, butter, oil, ointments or turmeric, and do not burst blisters.
6. Seek medical help for burns larger than the casualty's palm, deep burns, burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, burns in children and the elderly, chemical and electrical burns, and any breathing difficulty (airway burns from smoke).

**Chemical burns**: protect yourself; brush off dry powder; flood with plenty of running water for a long time; remove contaminated clothing.

**Electrical burns**: **switch off the current** before touching the casualty (or push away with a dry wooden object while standing on dry material); check breathing and start CPR if needed; cool entry and exit burns; always send to hospital (internal damage and heart rhythm problems).

## 10.11 Poisoning, bites and stings

### Poisoning
Poisons can be swallowed, inhaled, injected or absorbed through the skin.

1. Ensure your safety (gas, chemicals).
2. Find out what, how much and when; keep the container, label or vomit to show the doctor.
3. **Do not induce vomiting** — corrosives burn twice, and the person may inhale vomit.
4. For corrosives with a conscious casualty, rinse the mouth; do not try to neutralise.
5. Inhaled poisons (smoke, gas): move to fresh air if safe; open windows; no flames.
6. Skin contamination: remove clothes, wash with plenty of water. Eyes: irrigate.
7. If unconscious: recovery position, monitor breathing, CPR if needed (use a barrier — avoid mouth-to-mouth if the poison is on the lips).
8. Call 112/108 and take the casualty to hospital; poison information centres can advise.
9. Suspected pesticide (organophosphate) poisoning is common in India — remove contaminated clothes, wash the skin, keep the airway clear and transport quickly.

### Snake bite
**Do**: reassure (most bites are by non-venomous snakes, and calm reduces spread), keep the casualty still, **immobilise the bitten limb like a fracture** with a splint, remove rings, bangles and tight clothes, keep the limb at about heart level, note the time and the snake's appearance (do not try to catch or kill it), and **take the person to hospital quickly** where anti-snake venom is available.

**Do not**: tie a tight tourniquet, cut or suck the wound, apply ice, chemicals or herbal pastes, give alcohol, or waste time on traditional treatments.

(A memory aid used in Indian training: **Do it R.I.G.H.T.** — **R**eassure, **I**mmobilise, **G**o to hospital, **T**ell the doctor about symptoms on the way.)

### Dog and other animal bites
Wash the wound **immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water for about 15 minutes** — this greatly reduces the risk of rabies; do not apply chillies, oil or herbs; do not suture or tightly bandage; go to a health facility the same day for **anti-rabies vaccination** (and immunoglobulin when advised) and tetanus protection; observe the animal if possible.

### Insect stings (bees, wasps) and scorpion bites
- Bee sting: scrape the sting out sideways with a fingernail or card (squeezing injects more venom); wash; apply a cold pack; watch for anaphylaxis (multiple stings or stings in the mouth are dangerous).
- Scorpion sting: reassure, keep still, cold compress, take to hospital promptly (scorpion stings can be serious in children).

## 10.12 Frostbite and effects of heat

**Frostbite** (freezing of tissue — fingers, toes, ears, nose; seen in high-altitude regions): move to a warm place; remove wet clothing and rings; rewarm the part in warm (not hot) water, about body temperature, or by skin-to-skin contact; **do not rub** (damages tissue); do not rewarm if there is a chance of refreezing; cover loosely with dry dressings; get medical help. Treat **hypothermia** first if present — warm the whole body gradually with blankets and warm sweet drinks if conscious.

**Effects of heat**

| Condition | Signs | First aid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Heat cramps** | Painful muscle cramps after exertion in heat | Rest in shade, ORS or salted drinks, gentle stretching |
| **Heat exhaustion** | Heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, headache, dizziness, nausea, weak rapid pulse | Move to a cool place, lie down with legs raised, loosen clothing, sips of ORS or water, sponge with cool water; seek help if not better soon |
| **Heat stroke** (emergency) | Very high body temperature, hot dry (or sweaty) skin, confusion, seizures, unconsciousness | **Call 112/108**; move to shade; remove outer clothing; **cool rapidly** — wet the body with cool water and fan, or cold wet cloths/ice packs in the neck, armpits and groin; nothing by mouth if confused; recovery position if unconscious |

Prevention (as in national heat action plans): drink enough water, avoid strenuous work in the hottest hours, wear light loose clothing, check on the elderly and children.

## 10.13 Community emergencies

Floods, earthquakes, cyclones, landslides, fires, building collapse, stampedes, mass road accidents, industrial (chemical) accidents and epidemics.

**Role of the first aider and nurse**
1. **Preparedness**: know the disaster plan, emergency numbers, evacuation routes; keep a first-aid kit and emergency supplies; take part in mock drills (NDMA guidance).
2. **Scene safety and alerting**: do not rush in; report to 112/108, police, fire (101) and the disaster response team.
3. **Triage** — sorting casualties by urgency so that the most lives are saved. A common colour system:

| Colour | Category | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Red | Immediate — life-threatening but treatable | Airway problem, severe bleeding, shock |
| Yellow | Delayed — serious but stable | Fractures without shock |
| Green | Minor — "walking wounded" | Small cuts, bruises |
| Black | Dead or not expected to survive with available resources | No breathing after airway opened |

4. **First aid** for the injured, psychological first aid (listen, comfort, link to help), protection of vulnerable groups.
5. **Fire**: raise the alarm, evacuate (crawl low under smoke), use the stairs not the lift, use the correct extinguisher (PASS — Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep) only if safe; "stop, drop and roll" if clothes catch fire.
6. **Earthquake**: "drop, cover and hold on" indoors; stay away from windows; after shaking stops, move out carefully to an open area.
7. **Floods**: move to higher ground; avoid walking or driving through flood water; safe drinking water and food; prevent water-borne disease.
8. Record and hand over; support community recovery and rehabilitation.

## 10.14 The first-aid box (contents)

Sterile dressings and gauze pads, adhesive dressings of various sizes, roller and crepe bandages, triangular bandages, adhesive tape, cotton wool, safety pins, scissors, tweezers, disposable gloves, a face shield for rescue breaths, a thermometer, a torch, a clean cloth or cling film for burns, an eye pad, a cold pack, ORS packets, a notebook and pencil, and a list of emergency numbers. (Medicines are kept only as per the institution's policy and given by authorised persons.)

## Remember

- Aims: preserve life, prevent worsening, promote recovery; danger first; call 112 / 108.
- DR CAB: Danger, Response, Circulation (compressions), Airway, Breathing — check breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
- CPR: centre of chest, 5–6 cm, 100–120/min, full recoil, 30:2 or hands-only; AED as soon as available.
- Choking (adult): 5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts; infant: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts.
- Bleeding: firm direct pressure; tourniquet only for life-threatening limb bleeding.
- Shock: lie flat, legs up (if no injury), keep warm, nothing by mouth.
- Fracture: immobilise the joint above and below; RICE for sprains.
- Burns: cool running water for at least 20 minutes; cover with cling film; no ice, oil or toothpaste; Rule of Nines.
- Poisoning: do not induce vomiting; keep the container.
- Snake bite: reassure, immobilise, rush to hospital; no tourniquet, cutting or sucking. Dog bite: wash 15 minutes with soap and water, get anti-rabies vaccine.
- Heat stroke: rapid cooling and emergency help; frostbite: warm water, never rub.
- Triage: red immediate, yellow delayed, green minor, black dead or expectant.
